fields.title: The Mortification of Sin in Believers
fields.subtitle: On Killing Sin by the Spirit
fields.description: “Be killing sin or it will be killing you” is Owen's most quoted sentence, and this is the book it comes from. Written for students at Oxford who were making no progress against habits they hated, it refuses both easy answers: that a Christian should not have to fight, and that fighting harder is the answer. Owen works instead through what a besetting sin actually is, how it gains ground, and why only the Spirit can kill it — with a directness about self-deception that few writers before or since have matched.
fields.about_html:
Owen's subject is Paul's clause in Romans 8:13 — “if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” — and his thesis is the line everybody quotes: be killing sin, or it will be killing you. What follows is the most careful anatomy in English of how a besetting sin actually works, what pretends to be its cure, and why willpower and self-hatred are not the same thing as mortification.

It began as sermons to Oxford undergraduates while Owen was vice-chancellor of the university — young men, mostly, being told that sin is not managed by resolutions. That audience shows: the book is direct, unromantic, and assumes its hearers are already trying and already failing.

The book falls into three parts, and the third is the useful one: having established that the duty is lifelong and that the Spirit does the work, Owen turns to directions — how to load the conscience with the guilt of the sin, how to trace it back to what it actually wants, how to tell a wounded sin from a dead one. It is the section that reads least like theology and most like diagnosis.

Owen's prose is the hardest going of any book on this shelf; the sentences are long and the clauses stack. It is also the one readers most often say changed how they fight. Take it slowly — a section a sitting — and it opens.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
Christian Reader,

I shall tell you in a few words the reasons that won my consent to publishing the following discourse. The chief of them is the present state and condition of most of those who profess the faith: the visible evidence, in the state of their hearts and spirits, that they are badly unable to deal with the temptations surrounding them, arising both from the peace they have in the world and from the divisions they have among themselves. I am sure this is of such great importance that, if by this I only prompt others to press more effectively on people’s consciences the work of considering their ways, and to give clearer direction for reaching the goal proposed, I shall think well of my part in this undertaking. This was backed up by noticing the dangerous mistakes of some men who have lately taken it on themselves to give directions for the mortification of sin. Being unacquainted with the mystery of the gospel and the power of the death of Christ, they have once again laid the yoke of a self-made mortification on the necks of their disciples, a yoke which neither they nor their forefathers were ever able to bear. They cry up and press a mortification that matches that of the gospel neither in its nature, its subject, its causes, its means, nor its effects; and it constantly produces the sad results of superstition, self-righteousness and anxiety of conscience in those who take up the burden so bound on them.

What is offered here in weakness will, I humbly hope, agree with the spirit and letter of the gospel, and with the experience of those who know what it is to walk with God according to the terms of the covenant of grace. So if not this, then certainly something of this kind is very necessary at this time, to promote and advance this work of gospel mortification in the hearts of believers, and to direct them in paths that are safe and where they may find rest for their souls. I have something to add about what concerns me in particular. Having preached on this subject with some encouraging success, through the grace of Him who gives seed to the sower, I was urged by several people, in whose hearts are the ways of God, to publish what I had preached, with such additions and changes as I judged necessary. Moved by their wishes, I remembered the debt I have now owed for some years to several noble and worthy Christian friends: a treatise on Communion with God, promised to them some time ago. I then thought that, if I could not settle the greater debt by this, I might perhaps offer them this discourse of conflict with themselves as interest for their patience over that of peace and communion with God. Besides, I considered that in God’s providence I had been engaged in public debate over several controversies in religion, which might seem to call for something of another, more generally useful kind, as a fruit of choice rather than necessity. On these and similar grounds this short discourse is brought out to public view and now presented to you. I hope I may say sincerely that my heart’s desire to God, and the chief aim of my life in the position where God’s good providence has placed me, is that mortification and holiness in everything may be promoted in my own heart and in the hearts and ways of others, to the glory of God, so that the gospel of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ may be adorned in all things. If this little discourse (and this is the sum of the account I shall give of publishing it) may in any way be useful to the least of the saints toward that end, it will be seen as an answer to the weak prayers with which its unworthy author sends it out,

John Owen.

fields.title: The Foundation of the Whole Discourse, Laid in Romans 8:13
fields.body_html:
The foundation of the whole discourse laid in Rom. 8:13 — The apostle’s words explained — The certain connection between true mortification and salvation — Mortification the work of believers — The Spirit the chief agent of it — What is meant by “the body” in the apostle’s words — What by “the deeds of the body” — In what sense life is promised to this duty.

So that whatever direction I can offer toward carrying on the work of mortification in believers may be orderly and clear, I shall lay its foundation in the apostle’s words in Rom. 8:13, “If ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live,” and shall reduce the whole to an application of the great gospel truth and mystery they contain.

Having summed up his teaching on justification by faith, and the blessed state and condition of those who by grace share in it (verses 1–3 of this chapter), the apostle goes on to apply it to the holiness and comfort of believers.

Among his arguments and motives for holiness, this verse contains one drawn from the opposite outcomes and effects of holiness and sin: “If ye live after the flesh, ye shall die.” Since it is not my present aim to explain what it is to “live after the flesh” and what it is to “die,” I shall explain them only as far as they bear on the sense of the latter words of the verse, as stated above.

In the words chosen as the foundation of the following discourse, there is:

First, a duty commanded: “Mortify the deeds of the body.”

Secondly, the persons to whom it is commanded: “Ye,” “if ye mortify.”

Thirdly, a promise attached to that duty: “Ye shall live.”

Fourthly, the cause or means by which this duty is performed, the Spirit: “If ye through the Spirit.”

Fifthly, the conditional form of the whole statement, in which the duty, the means and the promise are contained: “If ye,” and so on.

1. The first thing we meet in the words, taken as a whole statement, is the conditional word Εἰ δὲ, “But if.” Conditionals in statements like this may signify two things:

(1.) The uncertainty of the outcome or thing promised, as far as the people to whom the duty is given are concerned. This is the case where the condition is absolutely necessary to the outcome, and does not itself depend on any definite cause known to the one to whom it is given. So we say, “If we live, we will do such a thing.” This cannot be the meaning of the conditional expression here. Of the people to whom these words are spoken it is said, in verse 1 of the same chapter, “There is no condemnation to them.”

(2.) The certainty of the link and connection between the things spoken of; as we say to a sick man, “If you take this medicine, or use this remedy, you will get well.” What we mean to express is solely the certainty of the connection between the medicine or remedy and health. And this is its use here. This conditional word points to the certain connection between mortifying the deeds of the body and living.

Now, things are connected in many ways, as cause and effect, or as means and end. The connection between mortification and life is not, properly and strictly, that of cause and effect, for “the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 6:23), but that of means and end. God has appointed this means for reaching the end He has freely promised. Means, though necessary, are fittingly subordinate to an end that is freely promised. A gift and a procuring cause in the one who receives it cannot go together. The meaning, then, of this statement as a conditional is that there is a certain, unfailing connection between true mortification and eternal life: if you use this means, you will reach that end; if you mortify, you will live. And in this lies the main motive and pressure behind the duty commanded.

2. The next thing we meet in the words is the persons to whom this duty is given. This is expressed in the word “Ye,” which in the original is contained in the verb θανατοῦτε, “if ye mortify”: that is, you believers; you for whom “there is no condemnation” (verse 1); you who are “not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (verse 9); who are “quickened by the Spirit of Christ” (verses 10, 11). It is to you that this duty is given. Pressing this duty directly on anyone else is a notable fruit of the superstition and self-righteousness the world is full of, the great work and aim of devout people who are ignorant of the gospel (Rom. 10:3–4; John 15:5). Now, this description of the persons, together with the command of the duty, is the main foundation of the following discourse, as it is stated in this thesis or proposition:

The choicest believers, who are certainly set free from the condemning power of sin, still ought to make it their business all their days to put to death the indwelling power of sin.

3. The chief agent in performing this duty is the Spirit: Εἰ δὲ Πνεύματι, “If by the Spirit.” The Spirit here is the Spirit mentioned in verse 11: the Spirit of Christ, the Spirit of God, who “dwells in us” (verse 9), who “quickens us” (verse 11); “the Holy Ghost” (verse 14); the “Spirit of adoption” (verse 15); the Spirit “that maketh intercession for us” (verse 26). All other ways of mortification are useless; all other helps leave us helpless. It must be done by the Spirit. People may attempt this work on other principles, as the apostle suggests in Rom. 9:30–32, by means and advantages supplied for other reasons, as they always have done and still do. But, he says, “This is the work of the Spirit. By Him alone is it to be done, and by no other power can it be brought about.” Mortification by one’s own strength, carried on by methods of one’s own invention, for the purpose of one’s own righteousness, is the soul and substance of all false religion in the world. And this is a second principle of the following discourse.

4. Next we must note the duty itself: “Mortify the deeds of the body.”

Three things need to be asked here: (1.) what is meant by the body; (2.) what by the deeds of the body; (3.) what by mortifying them.

(1.) The body at the end of the verse is the same as the flesh at the beginning: “If ye live after the flesh ye shall die; but if ye … mortify the deeds of the body,” that is, of the flesh. It is what the apostle has been discussing all along under the name of the flesh, as is clear from the way he carries through the contrast between the Spirit and the flesh, before and after. The body here, then, means that corruption and depravity of our nature of which the body is to a great extent the seat and instrument, the very members of the body being made servants of unrighteousness by it (Rom. 6:19). What is meant is indwelling sin, the corrupted flesh or lust. Many reasons could be given for this figure of speech, but I shall not dwell on them now. The “body” here is the same as παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος and σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας, the “old man” and the “body of sin” (Rom. 6:6). Or it may stand, as a part for the whole, for the whole person considered as corrupted, and as the seat of lusts and disordered affections.

(2.) The deeds of the body. The word is πράξεις, which does chiefly signify outward actions, “the works of the flesh,” as they are called, τὰ ἔργα τῆς σαρκός (Gal. 5:19), which are said there to be “manifest,” and are listed. Now, though only the outward deeds are mentioned here, their inward and immediate causes are chiefly meant. “The axe is to be laid to the root of the tree”: the deeds of the flesh are to be put to death in the causes from which they spring. The apostle calls them deeds because that is what every lust aims at. Even if it only conceives and miscarries, it aims to bring forth a complete sin.

Having dealt, both in the seventh chapter and at the beginning of this one, with indwelling lust and sin as the fountain and source of all sinful actions, he here speaks of its destruction under the name of the effects it produces. Πράξεις τοῦ σώματος are the same as φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός (Rom. 8:6), the “wisdom of the flesh,” by a figure of the same kind as the former; or as the παθήματα and ἐπιθυμίαι, the “passions and lusts of the flesh” (Gal. 5:24), from which its deeds and fruits arise. And it is in this sense that the body is used in Rom. 8:10: “The body is dead because of sin.”

(3.) To mortify. Εἰ θανατοῦτε, “If ye put to death”: a figure of speech taken from putting any living thing to death. To kill a man or any other living thing is to take away the source of all his strength, vigour and power, so that he cannot act or exert himself or do anything of his own. So it is in this case. Indwelling sin is compared to a person, a living person, called “the old man,” with his faculties and properties, his wisdom, craft, cunning and strength. This, says the apostle, must be killed, put to death, mortified; that is, its power, life, vigour and strength to produce its effects must be taken away by the Spirit. It is indeed completely put to death and slain by the cross of Christ, in merit and by way of example; and so the “old man” is said to be “crucified with Christ” (Rom. 6:6), and we ourselves to be “dead” with Him (verse 8). It is also really begun in regeneration (Rom. 6:3–5), when a principle contrary to it and destructive of it (Gal. 5:17) is planted in our hearts. But the whole work must be carried on by degrees toward perfection all our days. More of this as our discourse goes on. The apostle’s meaning in giving this command is that putting to death the indwelling sin that remains in our mortal bodies, so that it may not have life and power to bring forth the works or deeds of the flesh, is the constant duty of believers.

5. The promise attached to this duty is life: “Ye shall live.” The life promised is set against the death threatened in the clause before, “If ye live after the flesh, ye shall die,” which the same apostle expresses elsewhere as “He that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption” (Gal. 6:8), that is, destruction from God. Now, perhaps the word means not only eternal life but also the spiritual life in Christ that we have here; not as to its essence and being, which believers already enjoy, but as to its joy, comfort and vigour. As the apostle says in another case, “For now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8), that is, “Now my life will do me good; I shall have joy and comfort in my life.” So here: “You shall live; you shall lead a good, vigorous, comfortable, spiritual life while you are here, and obtain eternal life hereafter.”

Taking for granted what was said before about the connection between mortification and eternal life, as of means and end, I shall add only this, as a second motive to the duty commanded:

The vigour, power and comfort of our spiritual life depend on putting to death the deeds of the flesh.

fields.title: The Necessity of Mortification: The Duty of the Best Believers
fields.body_html:
The chief assertion about the necessity of mortification put forward for proof — Mortification the duty of the best believers, Col. 3:5; 1 Cor. 9:27 — Indwelling sin always remains; no perfection in this life, Phil. 3:12; 1 Cor. 13:12; 2 Pet. 3:18; Gal. 5:17, etc. — The activity of remaining sin in believers, Rom. 7:23; James 4:5; Heb. 12:1 — Its fruitfulness and tendency — Every lust aims at the extreme of its kind — The Spirit and the new nature given to fight against indwelling sin, Gal. 5:17; 2 Pet. 1:4–5; Rom. 7:23 — The fearful outcome of neglecting mortification, Rev. 3:2; Heb. 3:13 — The first general principle of the whole discourse confirmed by this — The lack of this duty lamented.

Having laid this foundation, a brief proof of the chief conclusions drawn above will lead me to what I mainly intend:

I. That the choicest believers, who are certainly set free from the condemning power of sin, still ought to make it their business all their days to put to death the indwelling power of sin.

So says the apostle in Col. 3:5: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth.” Whom is he speaking to? To those who were “risen with Christ” (verse 1); who were “dead” with Him (verse 3); whose life Christ was, and who would “appear with him in glory” (verse 4). You must put to death; make it your daily work; always be at it while you live; do not stop this work for a single day. Be killing sin, or it will be killing you. The fact that you are dead with Christ in principle, and made alive with Him, will not excuse you from this work. And our Saviour tells us how His Father deals with every branch in Him that bears fruit, every true and living branch: “He purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” (John 15:2). He prunes it, and not just for a day or two, but for as long as it is a branch in this world. And the apostle tells you what his own practice was: “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor. 9:27). “I do it daily,” he says. “It is the work of my life. I do not leave it out; this is my business.” And if this was the work and business of Paul, who was so incomparably raised above the ordinary measure of believers in grace, revelations, experiences, privileges and comforts, where can we possibly find grounds for an exemption from this work and duty while we are in this world? A brief account of the reasons for it may be given:

1. Indwelling sin always remains while we are in this world, so it must always be put to death. I am not dealing now with the empty, foolish and ignorant arguments of those who talk of keeping God’s commands perfectly, of perfection in this life, of being wholly and perfectly dead to sin. It is more than likely that the people who hold these abominable views never knew what it means to keep any one of God’s commands. They are so far below perfection of degree that they never reached even a perfection of parts in obedience, an obedience that is sincere in everything. And so many in our day who have talked of perfection have been more cunning, and have claimed that it consists in knowing no difference between good and evil. Not that they are perfect in the things we call good, but that everything is alike to them, and the height of wickedness is their perfection. Others have found a new way to it, by denying original, indwelling sin and toning down the spiritual demands of God’s law to suit people’s carnal hearts. As they have plainly shown themselves ignorant of the life of Christ and its power in believers, so they have invented a new righteousness the gospel knows nothing of, being vainly puffed up by their fleshly minds. As for us, who dare not be wise beyond what is written, nor boast through other people’s lives of what God has not done for us, we say that indwelling sin lives in us, in some measure and degree, while we are in this world. We dare not speak as “though we had already attained, either were already perfect” (Phil. 3:12). Our “inward man is renewed day by day” while we live here (2 Cor. 4:16), and the breaking down and decay of the old answers to the renewing of the new. While we are here we “know in part” (1 Cor. 13:12), having a remaining darkness that must be gradually removed by our growth “in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ” (2 Pet. 3:18). And “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit... so that ye cannot do the things that ye would” (Gal. 5:17), and so we fall short in our obedience as well as in our light (1 John 1:8). We have a “body of death” (Rom. 7:24), from which we are not delivered except by the death of our bodies (Phil. 3:21). Now, since it is our duty to put sin to death, to keep killing sin while it is in us, we must be at work. Someone appointed to kill an enemy does only half his work if he stops striking before the other stops living (Gal. 6:9; Heb. 12:1; 2 Cor. 7:1).

2. Sin not only still remains in us, but is still active, still labouring to bring forth the deeds of the flesh. When sin leaves us alone, we may leave sin alone. But sin is never less quiet than when it seems most quiet, and its waters are usually deep when they are still. So our plans against it should be vigorous at all times and in every condition, even where we least suspect it. Sin not only remains in us, but “the law in the members” is still “warring against the law of the mind” (Rom. 7:23), and “the spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy” (James 4:5). It is always at work: “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit” (Gal. 5:17); lust is always tempting and conceiving sin (James 1:14). In every moral action it is always either inclining us to evil, or holding us back from what is good, or putting the spirit out of tune for fellowship with God. It inclines us to evil: “The evil which I would not, that I do,” says the apostle (Rom. 7:19). Why is that? “Because in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing.” And it holds us back from good: “The good that I would I do not” (verse 19). “For the same reason, either I do not do it, or I do not do it as I should, all my holy things being defiled by this sin.” “The flesh lusteth against the Spirit... so that ye cannot do the things that ye would” (Gal. 5:17). And it puts our spirit out of tune, and so it is called “the sin which doth so easily beset us” (Heb. 12:1). This is why the apostle makes those grievous complaints about it in Romans 7. So sin is always active, always conceiving, always seducing and tempting. Who can say that he ever had anything to do with God or for God in which indwelling sin had no hand in corrupting what he did? And it will carry on this trade, more or less, all our days. If, then, sin will always be active, and we are not always putting it to death, we are lost. Someone who stands still and lets his enemies rain blow after blow on him without resistance will certainly be conquered in the end. If sin is cunning, watchful, strong and always at work on the business of killing our souls, and we are lazy, careless and foolish in going about its ruin, can we expect a happy outcome? There is not a day when sin does not either defeat or get defeated, prevail or be prevailed over; and it will be so as long as we live in this world.

I will release from this duty anyone who can bring sin to a settlement, to a ceasefire in this war. If it will spare him for one day, in any one duty (provided he is someone who understands the spiritual nature of obedience and the cunning of sin), let him say to his soul, as far as this duty goes, “Soul, take your rest.” The saints, whose souls long for deliverance from its troubling rebellion, know there is no safety against it except in constant warfare.

3. Sin will not only be striving, acting, rebelling, troubling and disturbing; if it is left alone, if it is not continually put to death, it will bring forth great, cursed, scandalous, soul-destroying sins. The apostle tells us what its works and fruits are in Gal. 5:19–21: “The works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like.” You know what it did in David and several others. Sin always aims at the extreme. Every time it rises up to tempt or entice, if it could have its own way, it would go on to the worst sin of that kind. Every unclean thought or glance would be adultery if it could; every covetous desire would be oppression; every thought of unbelief would be atheism, if it could grow to its full height. People may reach the point where sin is not heard speaking a scandalous word in their hearts, that is, urging them to some great sin with scandal openly in its mouth. Yet every stirring of lust, if it had its way, would go to the height of villainy. It is like the grave, which is never satisfied. And in this lies no small part of the deceitfulness of sin, by which it succeeds in hardening people and so ruins them (Heb. 3:13). It is modest, as it were, in its first stirrings and suggestions; but once it has got a foothold in the heart by them, it steadily holds its ground and presses on to further degrees of the same kind. This new activity and pressing forward makes the soul take little notice of how far a falling away from God has already begun. It thinks all is fairly well as long as there is no further progress. And as far as the soul is made insensible of any sin, that is, insensible in the way the gospel requires us to feel it, so far it is hardened. But sin is always pressing forward, because it has no limit except utter abandonment of God and opposition to Him. That it advances toward its height by degrees, holding the ground it has gained by hardening, comes not from its nature but from its deceitfulness. Now nothing can prevent this except mortification. That withers the root and strikes at the head of sin every hour, so that whatever it aims at, it is thwarted. There is not a saint in the world, even the best, who, if he gave up this duty, would not fall into as many cursed sins as anyone of his kind ever did.

4. This is one main reason why the Spirit and the new nature are given to us: so that we may have a principle within us by which to oppose sin and lust. “The flesh lusteth against the Spirit.” Well, and what then? “And the Spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). There is a tendency in the Spirit, or the spiritual new nature, to act against the flesh, just as there is in the flesh to act against the Spirit. So it is in 2 Pet. 1:4–5: it is our sharing in the divine nature that gives us escape from the corruption that is in the world through lust. And in Rom. 7:23 there is a law of the mind as well as a law of the members. Now, first, when two fighters are engaged, it is the most unjust and unreasonable thing in the world to tie one of them up and keep him from doing his utmost, and leave the other free to wound him as he pleases. And secondly, it is the most foolish thing in the world to tie up the one who fights for our eternal condition, and to leave alone the one who seeks and violently attempts our everlasting ruin. The contest is for our lives and souls. Not to be using the Spirit and the new nature every day to put sin to death is to neglect the excellent help God has given us against our greatest enemy. If we neglect to use what we have received, God may justly hold back from giving us more. His graces, as well as His gifts, are given to us to use, exercise and trade with. Not to be putting sin to death every day is to sin against the goodness, kindness, wisdom, grace and love of God, who has supplied us with a principle for doing it.

5. Negligence in this duty throws the soul into a condition exactly opposite to the one the apostle says was his: “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). In these people the inward man perishes, and the outward man is renewed day by day. Sin is like the house of David, and grace like the house of Saul. Exercise and success are the two main nourishers of grace in the heart. When it is allowed to lie idle, it withers and decays; the things that remain are ready to die (Rev. 3:2); and sin gains ground toward hardening the heart (Heb. 3:13). This is what I mean: by leaving out this duty, grace withers, lust flourishes, and the state of the heart grows worse and worse. And the Lord knows what desperate and fearful outcomes this has had with many. Where sin, through the neglect of mortification, wins a considerable victory, it breaks the bones of the soul (Ps. 31:10; 51:8), and makes a person weak, sick and ready to die (Ps. 38:3–5), so that he cannot look up (Ps. 40:12; Isa. 33:24). And when poor creatures will take blow after blow, wound after wound, defeat after defeat, and never rouse themselves to vigorous opposition, can they expect anything but to be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin, and for their souls to bleed to death (2 John 8)? Indeed, it is a sad thing to consider the fearful outcomes of this neglect, which lie before our eyes every day. Do we not see people whom we knew as humble, melting, broken-hearted Christians, tender and afraid to offend, zealous for God and all His ways, His Sabbaths and ordinances, who have grown earthly, carnal, cold and angry, through neglecting to watch over this duty, going along with the people and things of the world, to the scandal of religion and the fearful temptation of those who know them? The truth is that, between placing mortification in a rigid, stubborn state of mind (which is for the most part earthly, legalistic, judgmental and partial, and consistent with anger, envy, malice and pride) on the one hand, and claims of liberty, grace and who knows what on the other, true gospel mortification is almost lost among us. More of this later.

6. It is our duty to be “perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7:1); to be growing in grace every day (1 Pet. 2:2; 2 Pet. 3:18); to be renewing our inward man day by day (2 Cor. 4:16). Now, this cannot be done without putting sin to death every day. Sin sets its strength against every act of holiness and against every degree of growth we reach. Let no one think he is making any progress in holiness who does not walk over the bellies of his lusts. Whoever does not kill sin in this way takes no steps toward his journey’s end. Whoever finds no opposition from it, and does not set himself in every particular to put it to death, is at peace with it, not dying to it.

This, then, is the first general principle of the following discourse. In spite of the mortification of each and every sin by merit, if I may put it that way, in the cross of Christ; in spite of the real foundation for mortification in everything laid in our first conversion, through conviction of sin, humbling for sin, and the planting of a new principle opposite to it and destructive of it; sin still so remains, and so acts and works in the best of believers while they live in this world, that the constant daily putting of it to death is their duty all their days. Before I go on to consider the next principle, I cannot help complaining in passing about many who profess the faith in these days. Instead of bringing forth the great and evident fruits of mortification that might be expected, they hardly bear any leaves of it. There is indeed a broad light that has fallen on the people of this generation, and along with it many spiritual gifts have been given. These, with some other factors, have wonderfully enlarged the bounds of those who profess and of profession itself; both have multiplied and increased greatly. So there is a noise of religion and religious duties in every corner, and preaching in abundance, and that not in the empty, light, trivial and vain way of former times, but with a good measure of spiritual gift. So if you measure the number of believers by light, gifts and profession, the Church may have reason to say, “Who hath begotten me these?” But if you measure them by this great distinguishing grace of Christians, perhaps you will find their number not so multiplied. Where is the professing Christian who owes his conversion to these days of light, and so talks and professes at a level of spirituality that few in former days knew anything of (I will not judge them, though perhaps they boast of what the Lord has done in them), who does not show evidence of a miserably unmortified heart? If wasting time, idleness, uselessness in one’s position, envy, strife, quarrels, rivalry, anger, pride, worldliness and selfishness (1 Cor. 1) are badges of Christians, we have them on us and among us in abundance. And if it is like this with those who have much light, light we hope is saving, what shall we say of some who want to be thought religious and yet despise gospel light, and who know no more of the duty we are dealing with than what consists in people sometimes denying themselves outward pleasures, which is one of its outermost branches, and which they seldom practise anyway? May the good Lord send out a spirit of mortification to cure our disorders, or we are in a sad condition!

Two evils certainly come with every unmortified professing Christian: the first in himself, the other with respect to others.

1. In himself. Whatever he may claim, he has light thoughts of sin, at least of the sins of daily weakness. The root of an unmortified life is digesting sin without bitterness in the heart. When someone has trained his imagination to such a view of grace and mercy that he can swallow and digest daily sins without bitterness, he is on the very brink of turning the grace of God into lawlessness and being hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. There is no greater evidence in the world of a false and rotten heart than to carry on such a trade. To use the blood of Christ, which is given to cleanse us (1 John 1:7; Titus 2:14); the exaltation of Christ, which is to give us repentance (Acts 5:31); and the doctrine of grace, which teaches us to deny all ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12), to excuse sin, is a rebellion that in the end will break the bones. Most of the professing Christians who have fallen away in our day have gone out from us through this door. For a while most of them were under conviction. This kept them to their duties and brought them to profession, and so they “escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ” (2 Pet. 2:20). But having become familiar with the teaching of the gospel, and being weary of duty, for which they had no inner principle, they began to excuse themselves for many neglects on the basis of the doctrine of grace. And once this evil had taken hold of them, they quickly tumbled into perdition.

2. To others. It has an evil influence on them in two ways:

(1.) It hardens them, by persuading them that they are in as good a condition as the best professing Christians. Whatever they see in such people is so stained by the lack of this mortification that it means nothing to them. Such people have zeal for religion, but it comes with a lack of patience and of righteousness in everything. They reject extravagance, but with worldliness. They separate from the world, but live entirely for themselves, taking no care to show loving-kindness on the earth. Or they talk spiritually and live vainly; they speak of fellowship with God, and are in every way conformed to the world; they boast of forgiveness of sin and never forgive others. And with thoughts like these poor creatures harden their hearts in their unregenerate state.

(2.) It deceives them, by making them believe that if they can reach the same condition, all will be well with them. And so it becomes easy for them to wrestle with the great temptation of a religious reputation, when they may go far beyond such people in what shows outwardly, and yet fall short of eternal life. But more of these things, and of all the evils of an unmortified life, later.

fields.title: The Spirit Is the Only Author of This Work
fields.body_html:
The second general principle, about the means of mortification, put forward for proof — The Spirit the only author of this work — The emptiness of Roman Catholic mortification exposed — Many of the means they use not appointed by God — Those He has appointed misused — The mistakes of others in this matter — The Spirit promised to believers for this work, Ezek. 11:19; 36:26 — All we receive from Christ is by the Spirit — How the Spirit puts sin to death — Gal. 5:19–23 — The several ways He works to this end set out — How it is both His work and our duty.

The next principle concerns the great sovereign cause of the mortification we are dealing with. In the words laid as the foundation of this discourse, this is said to be the Spirit, that is, the Holy Ghost, as was shown.

II. He alone is sufficient for this work. All ways and means without Him are worth nothing; and He is the great agent of it, working in us as He pleases.

1. People look for other remedies in vain; they will not be healed by them. It is well known how many different ways have been prescribed for getting sin put to death. The greater part of the Roman Catholic religion, of what looks most like religion in their profession, consists of mistaken ways and means of mortification. This is the excuse for their rough garments, by which they deceive. Their vows, orders, fasts and penances are all built on this ground; they are all for the putting to death of sin. Their preaching, sermons and books of devotion all point this way. So those who interpret the locusts that came out of the bottomless pit (Rev. 9:3) as the friars of the Roman Church, who are said to torment people so “that men shall seek death, and shall not find it” (verse 6), think they did it by their stinging sermons. By these they convinced people of sin, but being unable to show them the remedy for healing and putting it to death, they kept them in such constant anguish and terror, and such trouble of conscience, that they wanted to die. This, I say, is the substance and glory of their religion. But between their labouring to put to death creatures that are already dead, ignorant of the nature and purpose of the work, and the poison they mixed into it in their belief in its merit, even supererogation (as they call their unnecessary merit, with a proud and barbarous title), their glory is their shame. But more of them and their mortification later, in chapter 7.

It is well known that the ways and means of putting sin to death that they invented are still urged and prescribed for the same purpose by some who should have more light and knowledge of the gospel. Directions of this kind have lately been given by some, and eagerly snatched up by others who profess to be Protestants, such as would have suited Roman Catholic devotees three or four hundred years ago. Such outward efforts, such bodily exercises, such self-performances, such purely legal duties, without the least mention of Christ or His Spirit, are varnished over with swelling words of vanity as the only means and methods for putting sin to death, in a way that shows a deep-rooted unfamiliarity with the power of God and the mystery of the gospel. Considering this was one reason for publishing this plain discourse.

Now, among other reasons why the Roman Catholics, with all their efforts, can never truly put any one sin to death, are these:

(1.) Because many of the ways and means they use and insist on for this purpose were never appointed by God for it. (Now, nothing in religion has any power to achieve an end unless it has it from God’s appointing it for that purpose.) Such are their rough garments, their vows, penances and disciplines, their course of monastic life, and the like. Of all these God will say, “Who hath required this at your hand?” and, “In vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” Of the same kind are various self-inflicted torments urged by others.

(2.) Because the things God has appointed as means, such as prayer, fasting, watching, meditation and the like, are not used by them in their proper place and order. These have their use in the matter in hand. But while they should all be regarded as streams, they treat them as the fountain. While they achieve their end only as means, subordinate to the Spirit and to faith, they suppose that they achieve it by the mere doing of the work. If they fast so much and pray so much and keep their hours and times, the work is done. As the apostle says of some in another case, they are “ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.” So these are always mortifying, but never come to any sound mortification. In a word, they have various means of putting to death the natural man, as to the natural life we live here, but none for putting to death lust or corruption.

This is the general mistake about this matter among people ignorant of the gospel, and it lies at the bottom of much of the superstition and self-made worship that has been brought into the world. What horrible self-torments some of the ancient founders of monastic devotion practised! What violence they did to nature! What extreme sufferings they put themselves through! Search their ways and principles to the bottom, and you will find they had no other root than this mistake: that in attempting rigorous mortification they fell upon the natural man instead of the corrupt old man, upon the body we live in instead of the body of death.

Nor will the natural popery that is in others do it. People are stung by the guilt of a sin that has prevailed over them. At once they promise themselves and God that they will never do it again. They watch over themselves and pray for a while, until this heat cools and the sense of sin wears off; and then mortification goes too, and sin returns to its former rule. Duties are excellent food for a healthy soul; they are no medicine for a sick soul. Someone who turns his food into his medicine must not expect it to do much. Spiritually sick people cannot sweat out their disease by working. But this is the way of people who deceive their own souls, as we shall see later.

That none of these ways is sufficient is clear from the nature of the work itself that is to be done. It is a work that requires so many things working together that no self-effort can reach it, and it is of such a kind that an almighty power is needed to accomplish it, as will be shown later.

2. It is, then, the work of the Spirit. For:

(1.) He is promised by God to be given to us to do this work. The taking away of the stony heart, that is, the stubborn, proud, rebellious, unbelieving heart, is in general the work of mortification we are dealing with. Now this is always promised to be done by the Spirit: “I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh” (Ezek. 11:19; 36:26). And this work is done by the Spirit of God when all other means fail (Isa. 57:17–18).

(2.) We have all our mortification as a gift from Christ, and all Christ’s gifts are communicated and given to us by the Spirit of Christ. “Without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5). All the supplies and relief that come from Him, in the beginning, growth and exercise of any grace whatever, come by the Spirit, through whom alone He works in and on believers. From Him we have our mortification: “Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance” (Acts 5:31), and our mortification is no small part of our repentance. How does He do it? Having “received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost,” He sends Him out for that purpose (Acts 2:33). You know the many promises He made of sending the Spirit, as Tertullian puts it, “Vicariam navare operam,” to carry out in His place the works He had to accomplish in us.

Answering one or two questions will now bring me closer to what I chiefly intend.

The first is, How does the Spirit put sin to death?

I answer, in general, in three ways:

[1.] By making our hearts abound in grace and in the fruits that are contrary to the flesh, its fruits, and their sources. So the apostle sets the fruits of the flesh against the fruits of the Spirit. “The works of the flesh,” he says, “are such and such” (Gal. 5:19–21); “but,” he says, “the fruit of the Spirit is quite contrary, of another sort altogether” (verses 22–23). Yes, but if these are in us and abound, may not the others abound too? No, he says in verse 24: “They that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.” But how? Verse 25: by living in the Spirit and walking in the Spirit; that is, by these graces of the Spirit abounding in us, and by walking according to them. For, says the apostle, “these are contrary the one to the other” (verse 17), so that they cannot both be in the same person in any intense or high degree. This “renewing of the Holy Ghost,” as it is called (Titus 3:5), is one great way of mortification. He makes us grow, thrive, flourish and abound in the graces that are contrary and opposed to, and destructive of, all the fruits of the flesh, and the quiet or thriving of indwelling sin itself.

[2.] By a real, physical working on the root and habit of sin, to weaken, destroy and remove it. So He is called “the spirit of judgment, and... the spirit of burning” (Isa. 4:4), really consuming and destroying our lusts. He takes away the stony heart by an almighty working; for as He begins the work in its kind, so He carries it on in its degrees. He is the fire that burns up the very root of lust.

[3.] He brings the cross of Christ into the heart of a sinner by faith, and gives us communion with Christ in His death and fellowship in His sufferings. More about how He does this later.

Secondly. If this is the work of the Spirit alone, why are we urged to do it? Since only the Spirit of God can do it, let the work be left entirely to Him.

[1.] It is the work of the Spirit in no other way than all the graces and good works in us are His. He “worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). He “hast wrought all our works in us” (Isa. 26:12), “the work of faith with power” (2 Thess. 1:11; Col. 2:12). He makes us pray, and is a “spirit of... supplications” (Rom. 8:26; Zech. 12:10). And yet we are urged, and should be urged, to all of these.

[2.] He does not work our mortification in us in such a way that it stops being an act of our obedience. The Holy Ghost works in us and on us as we are fit to be worked in and on; that is, in a way that preserves our own liberty and free obedience. He works on our understandings, wills, consciences and affections in keeping with their own natures. He works in us and with us, not against us or without us. So His help is an encouragement, making the work easier, and no excuse for neglecting the work itself. And indeed I might here lament the endless, foolish labour of poor souls who, being convinced of sin and unable to stand against the power of their convictions, set themselves to keep sin down by countless perplexing ways and duties, but all in vain, because they are strangers to the Spirit of God. They fight without victory, have war without peace, and are in slavery all their days. They spend their strength on what is not bread, and their labour on what does not profit.

This is the saddest warfare any poor creature can be engaged in. A soul under the power of conviction from the law is pressed to fight against sin, but has no strength for the fight. They cannot help fighting, and they can never win. They are like men thrust onto the swords of enemies on purpose to be killed. The law drives them on, and sin beats them back. Sometimes, indeed, they think they have defeated sin, when they have only raised a dust so that they cannot see it; that is, they stir up their natural feelings of fear, sorrow and anguish, which makes them believe that sin is conquered when it has not been touched. By the time they have cooled down, they must go back to the battle, and the lust they thought was killed turns out never to have been wounded.

And if the case is so sad for those who labour and strive and yet do not enter the kingdom, what is the condition of those who despise all this; who are always under the power and rule of sin and love to have it so; and who are troubled by nothing except that they cannot make enough provision for the flesh to fulfil its lusts?

fields.title: The Usefulness of Mortification to the Vigour of Our Spiritual Lives
fields.body_html:
The last principle: the usefulness of mortification — The vigour and comfort of our spiritual lives depend on our mortification — In what sense — Not absolutely and necessarily; Ps. 88, Heman’s condition — Not as on the next and immediate cause — As a means, by removing what is contrary — The desperate effects of any unmortified lust: it weakens the soul (Ps. 38:3, 8) in several ways, and darkens it — All graces strengthened by the putting to death of sin — The best evidence of sincerity.

The last principle I shall insist on (leaving aside, first, the necessity of mortification for life, and secondly, the certainty of life following mortification) is this:

III. That the life, vigour and comfort of our spiritual life depend greatly on our putting sin to death.

Strength and comfort, power and peace in our walk with God: these are the things we desire. If any of us were asked seriously what troubles us, we would have to put it under one of these headings: either we lack strength or power, vigour and life in our obedience, in our walk with God; or we lack peace, comfort and consolation in it. Whatever may happen to a believer that does not belong under one of these two headings does not deserve to be mentioned in the days of our complaints.

Now, all of these depend greatly on a constant course of mortification. On this, note:

1. I do not say they come from it as though they were necessarily tied to it. A person may be carried on in a constant course of mortification all his days, and yet perhaps never enjoy one good day of peace and consolation. So it was with Heman (Ps. 88). His life was one of constant mortification and walking with God, yet terrors and wounds were his portion all his days. But God singled out Heman, a choice friend, to make him an example to those who would later be in distress. Can you complain if it is no different with you than it was with Heman, that eminent servant of God? And this will be his praise to the end of the world. God makes it His own prerogative to speak peace and consolation (Isa. 57:18–19). “I will do that work,” says God; “I will... restore comforts unto him” (verse 18). But how? By a direct work of new creation: “I create” it, says God. The use of means to obtain peace is ours; the giving of it is God’s prerogative.

2. In the ways God has set up to give us life, vigour, courage and consolation, mortification is not one of the immediate causes. It is the privileges of our adoption, made known to our souls, that give us these things directly. “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God,” giving us a new name and a white stone; adoption and justification, that is, our sense and knowledge of them, are the immediate causes of these things, in the hand of the Spirit. But this I do say:

3. In our ordinary walk with God, and in His ordinary way of dealing with us, the vigour and comfort of our spiritual lives depend greatly on our mortification, not only as a “causa sine qua non” (a condition without which they cannot be), but as something that has a real influence on them. For:

(1.) This alone keeps sin from robbing us of both.

Every unmortified sin will certainly do two things: [1.] It will weaken the soul and rob it of its vigour. [2.] It will darken the soul and rob it of its comfort and peace.

[1.] It weakens the soul and robs it of its strength. When David had for a while harboured an unmortified lust in his heart, it broke all his bones and left him no spiritual strength. So he complained that he was sick, weak, wounded and faint. “There is,” he says, “no soundness in my flesh” (Ps. 38:3); “I am feeble and sore broken” (verse 8); “I am not able to look up” (Ps. 40:12). An unmortified lust will drink up the spirit and all the vigour of the soul, and weaken it for every duty. For:

1st. It puts the heart itself out of tune and out of order, by entangling its affections. It turns the heart away from the spiritual state that vigorous fellowship with God requires. It takes hold of the affections, making its object loved and desirable, and so drives out the love of the Father (1 John 2:15; 3:17), so that the soul cannot say honestly and truly to God, “You are my portion,” because it has something else it loves. Fear, desire and hope, the choicest affections of the soul, which ought to be full of God, will be entangled with it in one way or another.

2dly. It fills the thoughts with schemes about it. Thoughts are the great suppliers of the soul, bringing in provisions to satisfy its affections. And if sin remains unmortified in the heart, they must keep on making provision for the flesh, to fulfil its lusts. They must polish, adorn and dress up the objects of the flesh, and bring them home to give satisfaction; and in the service of a defiled imagination they can do this beyond all description.

3dly. It breaks out and actually hinders duty. The ambitious man must be studying, the worldling must be working or scheming, and the sensual, vain person must be supplying himself with vanity, when they ought to be engaged in the worship of God.

If it were my present business to set out the breaches, ruin, weakness and desolation that one unmortified lust will bring on a soul, this discourse would have to be extended far beyond what I intend.

[2.] As sin weakens the soul, so it darkens it. It is a cloud, a thick cloud, that spreads itself over the face of the soul and blocks every beam of God’s love and favour. It takes away all sense of the privilege of our adoption; and if the soul begins to gather up thoughts of consolation, sin quickly scatters them. More of this later.

Now, it is in this respect that the vigour and power of our spiritual life depend on our mortification: it is the only means of removing what will allow us neither of them. People who are sick and wounded under the power of lust try many remedies. They cry to God when the confusion of their thoughts overwhelms them; to God they cry, but they are not delivered. They use many remedies in vain: “Thou shalt not be cured.” So in Hos. 5:13: “When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah saw his wound,” they tried various remedies; nothing will work until they come (verse 15) to “acknowledge their offence.” People may see their sickness and wounds, but if they do not apply the right remedy, they will not be cured.

(2.) Mortification prunes all the graces of God and makes room for them to grow in our hearts. The life and vigour of our spiritual lives consists in the vigour and flourishing of the plants of grace in our hearts. Now, as you may see in a garden: plant a precious herb, leave the ground untilled, and let weeds grow around it, and perhaps it will still live, but it will be a poor, withering, useless thing. You must look and search for it, and sometimes can hardly find it; and when you do, you can hardly tell whether it is the plant you are looking for; and even if it is, you can make no use of it at all. But set another of the same kind in ground that is by nature just as barren and bad, and keep it well weeded, with everything harmful and damaging removed from it, and it flourishes and thrives. You can see it at your first glance into the garden, and have it for your use whenever you like. So it is with the graces of the Spirit planted in our hearts. It is true that they still exist; they remain in a heart where mortification is somewhat neglected. But they are ready to die (Rev. 3:2); they are withering and decaying. The heart is like the sluggard’s field, so overgrown with weeds that you can hardly see the good corn. Such a person may search for faith, love and zeal and hardly be able to find any. And if he does find that these graces are still there, alive and sincere, they are so weak and so choked with lusts that they are of very little use. They remain, indeed, but they are ready to die. But now let the heart be cleansed by mortification; let the weeds of lust be rooted up constantly and daily (for they spring up daily, nature being their natural soil); let room be made for grace to thrive and flourish; and how every grace will play its part, and be ready for every use and purpose!

(3.) As for our peace: just as nothing has any evidence of sincerity without mortification, so I know of nothing that carries such evidence of sincerity in it, and this is no small foundation of our peace. Mortification is the soul’s vigorous opposition to self, and in this sincerity is most evident.

fields.title: What It Is to Put a Sin to Death: What It Is Not
fields.body_html:
The main aim of the whole discourse set out — The first main case of conscience stated — What it is to put any sin to death, considered negatively — Not its complete destruction in this life — Not hiding it — Not improving some natural quality — Not diverting it — Not an occasional victory — Occasional victories over sin, what they are and when they happen: after an outbreak of sin; in a time of danger or trouble.

With these things laid down, I come to my main purpose: dealing with some questions or practical cases that arise in this business of believers putting sin to death.

The first, which heads all the rest and to which they can be reduced, may be stated as follows:

Suppose someone is a true believer, and yet finds in himself a powerful indwelling sin, taking him captive to its law, consuming his heart with trouble, confusing his thoughts, weakening his soul for the duties of fellowship with God, disturbing his peace, and perhaps defiling his conscience and exposing him to hardening through the deceitfulness of sin. What shall he do? What course shall he take and hold to for putting this sin, lust, disorder or corruption to death, to such a degree that, even though it is not completely destroyed, he may still be enabled in his fight with it to keep up power, strength and peace in fellowship with God?

In answer to this important question I shall do these things:

I. Show what it is to put any sin to death, both negatively and positively, so that we are not mistaken about the foundation.

II. Give general directions about the things without which it will be utterly impossible for anyone to get any sin truly and spiritually put to death.

III. Set out the particular steps by which this is to be done, keeping in mind throughout that I am dealing not with the doctrine of mortification in general, but only with the particular case stated above.

I. 1. (1.) To put a sin to death is not to kill it outright, root it out and destroy it, so that it has no hold or dwelling in our hearts at all. It is true that this is what we aim at, but it is not to be achieved in this life. No one who truly sets himself to put any sin to death fails to aim at, intend and desire its complete destruction, so that it leaves neither root nor fruit in the heart or life. He would like to kill it so thoroughly that it never moves or stirs again, never cries or calls, seduces or tempts, for all eternity. Its not existing is what he aims at. Now, though no doubt a wonderful success and remarkable victory over any sin may be gained by the Spirit and grace of Christ, so that a person may have almost constant triumph over it, yet its complete killing and destruction, so that it no longer exists, is not to be expected in this life. Paul assures us of this in Phil. 3:12: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect.” He was a choice saint, a pattern for believers, who in faith and love and all the fruits of the Spirit had no equal in the world, and on that account he claims perfection for himself in comparison with others (verse 15). Yet he had not “attained”; he was not “perfect,” but was “following after.” He still had a vile body, as we do, which must at last be changed by the great power of Christ (verse 21). This is what we would like; but God sees it best for us that we should be complete in nothing in ourselves, so that in everything we must be “complete in him” (Col. 2:10), which is best for us.

(2.) I think I need hardly say that it is not hiding a sin. When someone gives up the practice of some sin for outward reasons, people may perhaps regard him as a changed man. God knows that to his former wickedness he has added cursed hypocrisy, and has found a safer road to hell than the one he was on before. He has got a different heart from the one he had, one that is more cunning; not a new heart, one that is more holy.

(3.) The putting to death of sin does not consist in cultivating a quiet, calm nature. Some people have an advantage from their natural constitution, in that they are not exposed to such violent, unruly passions and stormy feelings as many others are. Now let such people cultivate and improve their natural disposition and temperament by discipline, reflection and prudence, and they may seem to themselves and to others to be very mortified people, when perhaps their hearts are a standing sewer of every abomination. One person is perhaps never troubled all his life by anger and passion, nor troubles others with it, as much as another is almost every day. And yet the second has done more toward putting that sin to death than the first. Let such people not test their mortification by things their natural temperament gives no life or vigour to. Let them set themselves against self-denial, unbelief, envy or some such spiritual sin, and they will get a truer view of themselves.

(4.) A sin is not put to death when it is only diverted. Simon Magus left his sorceries for a time, but the covetousness and ambition that drove him remained, and would have been at work in another way. So Peter tells him, “I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness.” “In spite of the profession you have made, and in spite of giving up your sorceries, your lust is as powerful in you as ever. It is the same lust; only its streams are diverted. It now shows itself and works in another way, but it is still the old gall of bitterness.” A person may be aware of a lust, set himself against its outbreaks, and take care that it does not break out as it has done, while all the time letting the same corrupt habit vent itself in some other way. He is like someone who heals and skins over a running sore and thinks he is cured, while meanwhile his flesh festers with the corruption of the same humour, and it breaks out in another place. And this diversion, with the changes that go with it, often happens to people for reasons that have nothing to do with grace. A change in one’s way of life, in relationships, interests or plans may bring it about. Even the changes in people’s constitutions that come naturally as their lives go on may produce changes like these. People in old age do not usually go on pursuing youthful lusts, even though they have never put a single one of them to death. And the same is true of trading lusts, giving up the service of one in order to serve another. Whoever exchanges pride for worldliness, sensuality for Pharisaism, or vanity in himself for contempt of others, let him not think he has put to death the sin he seems to have left. He has changed his master, but he is still a servant.

(5.) Occasional victories over sin do not amount to putting it to death.

There are two occasions or seasons when someone who is fighting any sin may seem to himself to have put it to death:

[1.] When it has had some grievous outbreak, disturbing his peace, terrifying his conscience, making him dread scandal, and plainly provoking God. This awakens and stirs up everything in the man and shocks him. It fills him with loathing of the sin and of himself for it; sends him to God; makes him cry out as if for his life, loathe his lust as he would hell, and set himself against it. With the whole man, spiritual and natural, now awake, sin pulls in its head and does not appear, but lies before him as if dead. It is like someone who has crept up to an army at night and killed one of its leaders: at once the guards wake up, men are roused, and a strict search is made for the enemy, who meanwhile hides, or lies like a dead man, until the noise and commotion are over, yet fully resolved to do the same mischief again at the next opportunity. Look at how the Corinthians mustered themselves to seize and destroy the sin among them (2 Cor. 7:11). So it is with a person when his lust, in some outbreak of actual sin, has broken through his conscience, his quiet, and perhaps his reputation. Carefulness, indignation, desire, fear and revenge are all set to work about it and against it, and lust is quiet for a while, run down before them. But when the commotion is over and the inquiry finished, the thief appears again, alive, and is as busy at his work as ever.

[2.] In a time of some judgment, disaster or pressing affliction. The heart is then taken up with thoughts and plans for escaping the present troubles, fears and dangers. A convinced person concludes that this can be done only by giving up sin, which gains peace with God. It is the anger of God in every affliction that galls a convinced person. To be rid of it, people at such times make resolutions against their sins. Sin will never again have any place in them; they will never again give themselves up to its service. And so sin is quiet; it does not stir; it seems to be put to death. Not that it has received a single wound, but merely because the soul has filled the faculties through which sin would act with thoughts that are inconsistent with its stirrings. When these thoughts are laid aside, sin comes back to its former life and vigour. The people in Ps. 78:32–37 are a full example and description of the state of mind I am speaking of: “For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works. Therefore their days did he consume in vanity, and their years in trouble. When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned and enquired early after God. And they remembered that God was their rock, and the high God their redeemer. Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues. For their heart was not right with him, neither were they stedfast in his covenant.” I have no doubt that when they sought, returned and enquired early after God, they did it with full purpose of heart to give up their sins; this is expressed in the word “returned.” To turn or return to the Lord means giving up sin. They did this “early,” that is, with earnestness and diligence. But their sin was still not put to death for all that (verses 36–37). And this is the state of many humblings in days of affliction, and a great deception in the hearts of believers themselves often lies here.

In these and many other ways poor souls deceive themselves, supposing they have put their lusts to death, when the lusts are alive and mighty, and break out on every occasion to their disturbance and unrest.

fields.title: Putting a Particular Sin to Death Described
fields.body_html:
Putting sin to death described in particular — Its several parts and degrees — The settled weakening of its root and principle — The power of lust to tempt — How that power differs between persons and times — Constant fighting against sin — Its parts considered — Success against it — The sum of this discourse considered.

Next we must consider what it is to put a sin to death in general, which will prepare the way further for particular directions.

2. Putting a lust to death consists in three things:

(1.) A settled weakening of it. Every lust is a depraved habit or disposition, continually inclining the heart to evil. Hence the description, in Gen. 6:5, of someone who has no lust truly put to death: “Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” He is always under the power of a strong bent and inclination to sin. And the reason why a natural man is not always pursuing some one lust, night and day, is that he has many to serve, each crying out to be satisfied. So he is carried along with great variety, but in general he always leans toward satisfying himself.

Let us suppose, then, that the lust or disorder we are asking how to put to death is in itself a strong, deep-rooted, settled inclination and bent of the will and affections toward some actual sin, as to its substance, even though it is not always, considered formally, stirring up imaginations, thoughts and schemes about its object. So people are said to have their “hearts set upon evil”; the bent of their spirits lies toward it, to make “provision for the flesh.” And a sinful, depraved habit differs, in this as in many other things, from every natural or moral habit. Whereas those incline the soul gently and in keeping with its nature, sinful habits drive it with violence and force. So lusts are said to “war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2:11); to rebel, or rise up in war, with the strategy and opposition usual in war (Rom. 7:23); to lead captive, or actually to take captive after success in battle. All these are works of great violence and force.

I could show fully, from the description we have of it in Romans 7, how it darkens the mind, snuffs out convictions, dethrones reason, cuts off the power and influence of any considerations that may be brought to restrain it, and breaks through everything into a flame. But that is not my present business. Now, the first thing in mortification is the weakening of this habit of sin or lust, so that it does not rise up, conceive, riot, provoke, entice and disturb with the violence, earnestness and frequency it naturally tends to (James 1:14–15).

I would like to give one caution or rule in passing, and it is this: though every lust by its own nature inclines and drives to sin equally and in every case, this must be granted with these two limits:

[1.] One lust, or a lust in one person, may receive many incidental boosts, heightenings and strengthenings that give it life, power and vigour far beyond what another lust has, or what the same lust (that is, of the same kind and nature) has in another person. When a lust falls in with someone’s natural constitution and temperament, with a suitable way of life, or with opportunities, or when Satan has got a convenient handle on it to manage it (and he has a thousand ways of doing so), that lust grows violent and forceful beyond others, or beyond the same lust in another person. Then its fumes so darken the mind that, though the person knows the same things as before, they have no power or influence on the will, and corrupt affections and passions are set free by it.

But above all, lust gains strength through temptation. When a suitable temptation falls in with a lust, it gives it a new life, vigour, power, violence and rage that it did not seem to have, or to be capable of, before. Examples of this could be multiplied, but showing this is the aim of part of another treatise.

[2.] Some lusts are far more noticeable and discernible than others in their violent workings. Paul makes a distinction between sexual sin and all other sins: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). So the stirrings of that sin are more noticeable and discernible than those of others, while perhaps the love of the world or the like is no less habitually dominant in a person, yet does not cause such an uproar in the whole person.

And for this reason some people may pass, in their own thoughts and in the eyes of the world, for mortified people, who still have in them no less dominance of lust than those who cry out in alarm at its troubling riots, or even those who have been driven by its power into scandalous sins. It is only that their lusts are in and about things that do not raise such a commotion in the soul, things they deal with in a calmer state of mind, because the very fabric of nature is not so closely involved in them as in some others.

I say, then, that the first thing in mortification is the weakening of this habit, so that it does not drive and riot as it used to; so that it does not entice and draw aside; so that it does not disturb and confuse; the killing of its life, vigour, quickness and readiness to stir. This is called crucifying “the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal. 5:24), that is, taking away the blood and spirits that give it strength and power; the wasting away of the body of death “day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

It is like a man nailed to the cross. At first he struggles and strives and cries out with great strength and might; but as his blood and spirits drain away, his struggles become faint and rare, and his cries low and hoarse, hardly to be heard. So when someone first takes on a lust or disorder to deal with it, it struggles with great violence to break loose; it cries out with earnestness and impatience to be satisfied and relieved. But when its blood and spirits are let out by mortification, it moves rarely and faintly, cries out seldom, and is hardly heard in the heart. It may sometimes have a dying spasm that gives an appearance of great vigour and strength, but that is soon over, especially if it is kept from any significant success. The apostle describes this in the whole of Romans 6, but especially in verse 6.

“Sin,” he says, “is crucified; it is fastened to the cross.” For what purpose? “That the body of sin might be destroyed,” the power of sin weakened and abolished little by little, “that henceforth we should not serve sin,” that is, that sin might not incline and drive us so effectively as to make us its servants, as it has done before. And this is said not only of carnal and sensual affections, or desires for worldly things, not only of the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, but also of the flesh as it is in the mind and will, in that opposition to God that is in us by nature. Whatever kind the troubling disorder may be, and in whatever ways it shows itself, whether by driving to evil or by holding back from what is good, the rule is the same. Unless this is done effectively, all later fighting will not reach the goal aimed at. A man may knock the bitter fruit off an evil tree until he is weary; while the root remains in strength and vigour, knocking down the present fruit will not stop it bearing more. This is the folly of some people: they set themselves with all earnestness and diligence against the visible outbreaks of lust, but because they leave the principle and root untouched, and perhaps unsearched, they make little or no progress in this work of mortification.

(2.) In constant fighting and struggling against sin. To be able always to be laying blows on sin is no small degree of mortification. When sin is strong and vigorous, the soul is hardly able to make any stand against it. It sighs and groans and mourns and is troubled, as David says of himself, but it seldom has sin on the run. David complains that his iniquities had “taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up” (Ps. 40:12). How little, then, was he able to fight against it! Now, several things are required for this fighting against sin and are included in it:

[1.] It requires a person to know that he has such an enemy to deal with; to take notice of it; to regard it as an enemy indeed, one to be destroyed by every possible means. As I said before, the contest is vigorous and dangerous; it concerns the things of eternity. So when people have light and passing thoughts of their lusts, it is no great sign that they are mortified, or on the way to mortification. This is each person’s knowing “the plague of his own heart” (1 Kings 8:38), without which no other work can be done. It is to be feared that very many know little of the main enemy they carry about with them in their bosoms. This makes them ready to justify themselves and impatient of rebuke or warning, not knowing that they are in any danger (2 Chron. 16:10).

[2.] Working to become familiar with the ways, tricks, methods, advantages and occasions of its success is the beginning of this warfare. This is how people deal with enemies. They find out their counsels and plans, ponder their aims, and consider how and by what means they have prevailed before, so that they may be forestalled. The greatest skill in generalship consists in this. Take it away, and all waging of war, where human wisdom and industry are most fully used, would be mere brute force. So do those deal with lust who really put it to death. Not only when it is actually vexing, enticing and seducing, but in their quiet times they consider: “This is our enemy; this is his way and his progress; these are his advantages; this is how he has prevailed, and this is what he will do if he is not forestalled.” So David says, “My sin is ever before me” (Ps. 51:3). And indeed one of the choicest and most eminent parts of practical spiritual wisdom consists in finding out the subtleties, policies and depths of any indwelling sin: to consider and know where its greatest strength lies; what advantage it usually takes of occasions, opportunities and temptations; what its pleas, pretexts and reasonings are; what its stratagems, disguises and excuses are; to set the wisdom of the Spirit against the craft of the old man; to trace this serpent through all its turnings and windings; to be able to say, at its most secret workings, which an ordinary heart would not notice, “This is your old way and course; I know what you are aiming at.” To be always ready like this is a good part of our warfare.

[3.] To load it daily with all the things mentioned later, which are grievous, deadly and destructive to it, is the height of this contest. Such a person never thinks his lust is dead because it is quiet, but keeps working to give it new wounds and new blows every day. So the apostle says in Col. 3:5.

Now, while the soul is in this condition, while it is dealing with sin like this, it is certainly on top. Sin is under the sword and dying.

(3.) In success. Frequent success against any lust is another part and evidence of mortification. By success I mean not merely that sin is frustrated, so that it is not brought forth or accomplished, but a victory over it, and pursuing it to complete conquest. For example, when the heart finds sin at work at any time, seducing and forming imaginations to make provision for the flesh, to fulfil its lusts, it at once arrests sin, brings it before the law of God and the love of Christ, condemns it, and follows through with its execution to the uttermost.
