Now, I say, when someone comes to this state and condition, where lust is weakened in its root and principle, and its stirrings and actions are fewer and weaker than before, so that they cannot hinder his duty or interrupt his peace; when he can find sin out and fight against it in a quiet, calm state of mind, and have success against it; then sin is put to death in some considerable measure, and in spite of all its opposition a person may have peace with God all his days.

To these headings, then, I refer the mortification aimed at, that is, of any one troubling disorder through which the general depravity and corruption of our nature tries to show itself and break out:

First, the weakening of its indwelling disposition, by which it inclines, entices and drives to evil, and rebels, opposes and fights against God, is the foundation of it. This happens by the planting, settled dwelling and nourishing of a principle of grace that stands in direct opposition to it and destroys it. So pride is weakened by the planting and growth of humility, passion by patience, impurity by purity of mind and conscience, love of this world by heavenly-mindedness. These are graces of the Spirit, or the same settled grace working in different ways by the Holy Ghost according to the variety of objects it is exercised on; just as the others are several lusts, or the same natural corruption working in different ways according to the various advantages and occasions it meets. A second thing required is the quickness, eagerness and vigour of the Spirit, or new man, in struggling with and cheerfully fighting against the lust in question, by all the ways and with all the means appointed for it, constantly using the help provided against its stirrings and workings. Success to various degrees goes with these two. Now this, unless the disorder has an unconquerable advantage from its natural situation, may possibly reach such a complete conquest that the soul never again noticeably feels its opposition; and in any case it will certainly reach the point of granting peace to the conscience, according to the terms of the covenant of grace.

fields.title: General Rules, without Which No Lust Will Be Put to Death
fields.body_html:
General rules without which no lust will be put to death — No mortification unless a person is a believer — The dangers of unregenerate people attempting to put sin to death — The duty of unconverted people in this matter of mortification considered — The emptiness of the Roman Catholics’ attempts and rules for mortification exposed by this.

II. Next we must consider the ways and means by which a soul may go about putting to death any particular lust and sin that Satan uses to disturb and weaken him.

Now, some general considerations must be laid down first, about certain principles and foundations of this work. Without them no one in the world, however much stirred up by convictions and determined to put any sin to death, can achieve it.

The general rules and principles without which no sin will ever be put to death are these:

1. Unless a person is a believer, that is, one truly grafted into Christ, he can never put any one sin to death. I do not say unless he knows himself to be one, but unless he really is one.

Mortification is the work of believers. “If ye through the Spirit” (Rom. 8:13), and so on: you believers, for whom there is no condemnation (verse 1). They alone are urged to it: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3:5). Who should put to death? You who are “risen with Christ” (verse 1); whose “life is hid with Christ in God” (verse 3); who “shall appear with him in glory” (verse 4). An unregenerate person may do something like it, but he can never perform the work itself in a way acceptable to God. You know what a picture of it some of the philosophers drew: Seneca, Tully, Epictetus. What moving discourses they have on contempt of the world and of self, on regulating and conquering every excessive affection and passion! The lives of most of them showed that their maxims differed from true mortification as much as a sun painted on a signpost differs from the sun in the sky; they had neither light nor heat. Their own Lucian shows plainly enough what they all were. There is no death of sin without the death of Christ. You know what attempts the Roman Catholics make at it, in their vows, penances and satisfactions. I dare say of them (I mean as many of them as act on the principles of their church, as they call it) what Paul says of Israel regarding righteousness (Rom. 9:31–32): they have followed after mortification, but have not attained it. Why? “Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law.” The same is the state and condition of all among ourselves who, in obedience to their convictions and awakened consciences, attempt to give up sin. They follow after it, but they do not attain it.

It is true that it is, and will be, required of every person who hears the law or the gospel preached that he put sin to death. It is his duty, but it is not his first duty. It is his duty to do it, but to do it in God’s way. If you tell your servant to pay a certain sum for you at a certain place, but first to go and collect it at another, it is his duty to pay the money as directed, and you will blame him if he does not. Yet it was not his first duty; he was first to collect it, according to your directions. So it is in this case. Sin is to be put to death, but something must be done first to enable us to do it.

I have proved that it is the Spirit alone who can put sin to death. He is promised to do it, and all other means without Him are empty and useless. How, then, can someone who does not have the Spirit put sin to death? A person could more easily see without eyes or speak without a tongue than truly put one sin to death without the Spirit. Now, how is He obtained? He is the Spirit of Christ. And as the apostle says, “If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his” (Rom. 8:9), so if we are Christ’s and have a share in Him, we have the Spirit, and so we alone have power for mortification. The apostle discusses this at length: “So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. 8:8). This is the inference and conclusion he draws from his preceding discussion of our natural state and condition, and the hostility toward God and His law that we have in it. If we are in the flesh, if we do not have the Spirit, we cannot do anything that pleases God. But what is our deliverance from this condition? Verse 9: “But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you.” “You believers, who have the Spirit of Christ, are not in the flesh.” There is no way of deliverance from the state and condition of being in the flesh except by the Spirit of Christ. And what if this Spirit of Christ is in you? Why, then you are mortified: “The body is dead because of sin” (verse 10), or dead to it. Mortification is carried on; the new man is made alive to righteousness. The apostle proves this in verse 11 from the union we have with Christ by the Spirit, which will produce in us workings that match what it worked in Him. All attempts, then, to put any lust to death without a share in Christ are useless. Many people who are stung with and for sin, when the arrows of Christ for conviction have been made sharp in their hearts by the preaching of the word or by some affliction, vigorously set themselves against this or that particular lust that has most disturbed or troubled their consciences. But, poor creatures, they labour in the fire, and their work is burned up. When the Spirit of Christ comes to this work, He will be “like a refiner’s fire, and like fullers’ soap,” and He will purify people like gold and silver (Mal. 3:2–3), taking away their dross and tin, their filth and blood, as in Isa. 4:4. But people must be gold and silver at bottom, or refining will do them no good. The prophet gives us the sad outcome of wicked people’s utmost attempts at mortification, by whatever means God gives them: “The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain... Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the Lord hath rejected them” (Jer. 6:29–30). And why is this? Verse 28: they were “brass and iron” when they were put into the furnace. People may refine brass and iron for a long time before it becomes good silver.

I say, then, that mortification is not the present business of unregenerate people. God does not call them to it yet. Conversion is their work, the conversion of the whole soul, not the putting to death of this or that particular lust. You would laugh at a man if you saw him putting up a great building and never taking any care over a foundation; especially if you saw him so foolish that, after a thousand experiences of what he built one day falling down the next, he still kept on the same way. So it is with convinced people. Though they plainly see that the ground they gain against sin one day they lose the next, they still go on along the same road, without asking where the destructive flaw in their progress lies. When the Jews, convicted of their sin, were cut to the heart and cried out, “What shall we do?” (Acts 2:37), what did Peter tell them to do? Did he tell them to go and put to death their pride, anger, malice, cruelty and the like? No; he knew that was not their present work. He called them to conversion and faith in Christ in general (verse 38). Let the soul first be thoroughly converted, and then, as they “look upon me whom they have pierced,” humbling and mortification will follow. So when John came to preach repentance and conversion, he said, “Now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees” (Matt. 3:10). The Pharisees had been laying heavy burdens, imposing tedious duties and rigid means of mortification, in fasts, washings and the like, all in vain. John says, “The doctrine of conversion is for you; the axe in my hand is laid to the root.” And our Saviour tells us what must be done in this case. “Do men gather grapes of thorns?” He asks (Matt. 7:16). But suppose a thorn is well pruned and cut, and pains are taken with it? “Yes, but it will never bear figs” (verses 17–18). Every tree is bound to bear fruit according to its own kind. What, then, must be done? He tells us in Matt. 12:33: “Make the tree good, and his fruit good.” The root must be dealt with and the nature of the tree changed, or no good fruit will be produced.

This is my point: unless a person is regenerate, unless he is a believer, all the attempts he can make at mortification, however impressive and promising, and all the means he can use, however diligently, earnestly, watchfully and intently he follows them, are to no purpose. He will use many remedies in vain; he will not be healed. Indeed, several desperate evils come with the efforts of convinced people, who are nothing more than that, to perform this duty:

(1.) The mind and soul are taken up with what is not the person’s proper business, and so he is turned aside from what is. God by His word and judgments takes hold of some sin in him, stings his conscience, disturbs his heart and robs him of his rest. Now other distractions will not serve; he must apply himself to the work in front of him. The business at hand is to awaken the whole person to consider the state and condition he is in, so that he may be brought home to God. Instead of this he sets himself to put to death the sin that stings him, which springs purely from self-love, from wanting to be free of his trouble, and has nothing to do with the work he is called to. And so he is turned aside from it. So God tells us of Ephraim, when He “spread my net upon them; I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven; I will chastise them” (Hos. 7:12): caught them, entangled them, convinced them that they could not escape. He says of them, “They return, but not to the most High” (verse 16). They set themselves to give up sin, but not in the way God called for, by conversion of the whole person. So people are turned aside from coming to God by the most glorious ways they can settle on for coming to Him. And this is one of the most common deceptions by which people ruin their own souls. I wish that some whose trade it is to plaster with untempered mortar in the things of God did not teach this deception and lead the people astray by their ignorance. What do people do, and what are they often directed to do, when their consciences are stung by sin and by unrest from the Lord who has taken hold of them? Is not the sum of what they apply themselves to a giving up, in practice, of the sin whose fruits trouble them, and a making of a stand against it? And is not the gospel purpose of their convictions lost in this way? Here people stay and perish.

(2.) Since this duty is good in itself, in its proper place, a duty that shows sincerity and brings peace home to the conscience, a person who finds himself really engaged in it, with his mind and heart set against this or that sin and a purpose and resolution to have nothing more to do with it, is ready to conclude that his state and condition is good, and so deludes his own soul. For:

[1.] When his conscience has been made sick with sin and he could find no rest, at the very moment he should go to the great Physician of souls and get healing in His blood, the man calms and quiets his conscience by this campaign against sin, and sits down without going to Christ at all. Ah, how many poor souls are deluded like this for eternity! “When Ephraim saw his sickness... then went Ephraim to the Assyrian, and sent to king Jareb” (Hos. 5:13), and this kept him away from God. The whole bundle of the Roman religion is made up of schemes and devices for calming conscience without Christ, all described by the apostle in Rom. 10:3.

[2.] In this way people satisfy themselves that their state and condition is good, since they are doing a work that is good in itself, and are not doing it to be seen. They know they want the work done in sincerity, and so they are hardened in a kind of self-righteousness.

(3.) When someone has been deluded like this for a while, and has deceived his own soul, and finds over a long course of life that his sin is really not put to death, or that if he has changed one sin he has picked up another, he begins at last to think that all fighting is in vain. He will never be able to prevail; he is building a dam against water that keeps rising on him. And so he gives up, as one despairing of any success, and surrenders himself to the power of sin and to the habit of empty formality he has acquired.

And this is the usual outcome for people who attempt to put sin to death without first obtaining a share in Christ. It deludes them, hardens them and destroys them. That is why we see that there are usually no more vile and desperate sinners in the world than those who were set on this course by conviction, found it fruitless, and abandoned it without discovering Christ. And this is the substance of the religion and godliness of the choicest formalists in the world, and of all those who in the Roman church are driven to mortification as they drive Indians to baptism or cattle to water. I say, then, that mortification is the work of believers, and of believers only. Killing sin is the work of living people. Where people are dead (as all unbelievers, even the best of them, are dead), sin is alive, and will go on living.

2. It is the work of faith, the special work of faith. Now, if there is a work to be done that can be accomplished by only one instrument, it is the height of madness for anyone who does not have that instrument to attempt it. And it is faith that purifies the heart (Acts 15:9); or, as Peter says, we have “purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit” (1 Pet. 1:22). Without it, it will not be done.

What has been said is, I suppose, enough to establish my first general rule: Be sure to get a share in Christ. If you intend to put any sin to death without it, it will never be done.

Objection. You will say, “What, then, would you have unregenerate people do who are convinced of the evil of sin? Should they stop striving against sin, live dissolutely, give their lusts free rein, and be as bad as the worst of people? That would throw the whole world into confusion, bring everything into darkness, open the floodgates of lust, and drop the reins on people’s necks, so that they rush into every sin with delight and greed, like a horse into battle.”

Answer. 1. God forbid! It should be seen as a great result of God’s wisdom, goodness and love that by many ways and means He is pleased to restrain the children of men from running out into the full range of excess and riot that the depravity of their nature would violently carry them to. In whatever way this is done, it is a result of God’s care, kindness and goodness, without which the whole earth would be a hell of sin and confusion.

2. There is a special convicting power in the word, which God is often pleased to put out, to wound, shock and in some way humble sinners, even though they are never converted. And the word is to be preached even though it has this result, though not with this as its aim. Let the word, then, be preached, and people’s sins will be rebuked, lust will be restrained, and some stand will be made against sin, though that is not the effect aimed at.

3. Though this is the work of the word and the Spirit, and is good in itself, it is not profitable or effective for the main purpose in those in whom it is worked. They are still in the gall of bitterness and under the power of darkness.

4. Let people know it is their duty, but in its proper place. I am not taking people away from mortification, but setting them on to conversion. Someone who calls a man away from mending a hole in the wall of his house to put out a fire that is consuming the whole building is not his enemy. Poor soul! It is not your sore finger but your wasting fever that you need to turn your attention to. You set yourself against one particular sin, and do not consider that you are nothing but sin.

Let me add this for those who are preachers of the word, or who intend that work, through the good hand of God. It is their duty to plead with people about their sins, and to bear down on particular sins. But they should always remember to do it with the proper purpose of law and gospel in view; that is, they should use the sin they speak against to expose the state and condition the sinner is in. Otherwise they may perhaps bring people to formality and hypocrisy, but little of the true purpose of preaching the gospel will be achieved. It is no use beating a man out of his drunkenness into a sober formality. A skilful master of the assemblies lays his axe at the root and always presses on to the heart. To speak out against the particular sins of ignorant, unregenerate people, of whom the land is full, is a good work. But even if it is done with great power, vigour and success, if all it achieves is that they set themselves to the most diligent efforts to put to death the sins preached against, all that is done is like beating an enemy in the open field and driving him into a fortress that cannot be taken. Have you ever got a sinner at an advantage over any one sin at all? Have you anything to take hold of him by? Bring it to bear on his state and condition, drive it up to the head, and deal with him there. To break people off particular sins without breaking their hearts is to throw away our advantages in dealing with them.

And in this Roman mortification is grievously at fault. They drive all kinds of people to it, without the slightest thought of whether they have a principle for it or not. Indeed, they are so far from calling people to believe so that they may be able to put their lusts to death that they call people to mortification instead of believing. The truth is that they know neither what it is to believe nor what mortification itself means. Faith for them is only a general assent to the doctrine taught in their church; and mortification is a person committing himself by a vow to some particular way of life, in which he denies himself some use of the things of this world, not without considerable compensation. Such people know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Their boasting of their mortification is only glorying in their shame. Some writers on cases of conscience among ourselves, who overlook the necessity of regeneration, openly give this direction to all kinds of people who complain of any sin or lust: that they should vow against it, at least for a time, a month or so. These seem to have a scrap of light in the mystery of the gospel, much like that of Nicodemus when he first came to Christ. They tell people to vow to abstain from their sin for a time. This usually makes their lust more forceful. Perhaps, with great anguish, they keep their word; perhaps not, which increases their guilt and torment. Is their sin put to death at all by this? Do they find a victory over it? Is their condition changed, even if they manage to give it up? Are they not still in the gall of bitterness? Is this not to set people making bricks, if not without straw, then, which is worse, without strength? What promise does any unregenerate person have to support him in this work? What help to perform it? Can sin be killed without a share in the death of Christ, or put to death without the Spirit? Even if such directions should succeed in changing people’s lives, as they seldom do, they never reach to the change of their hearts or condition. They may make people self-justifiers or hypocrites, but not Christians. It often grieves me to see poor souls who have a zeal for God and a desire for eternal welfare kept by such directors and directions, all their days, under a hard, burdensome, outward worship and service of God, with many impressive efforts at mortification, in complete ignorance of the righteousness of Christ and unfamiliarity with His Spirit. I know too many people and things of this kind. If God ever shines into their hearts, to give them the knowledge of His glory in the face of His Son Jesus Christ, they will see the folly of their present way.

fields.title: Without Sincerity in Everything, No Single Lust Will Be Put to Death
fields.body_html:
The second general rule set out — Without sincerity in putting every lust to death, no lust will be put to death — Partial mortification always comes from a corrupt principle — The troubling temptation of one lust often a chastening for other neglects.

2. The second principle I shall put forward for this purpose is this:

Without sincerity and diligence in obedience in everything, no mortification of any one troubling lust can be obtained.

The first principle concerned the person; this one concerns the thing itself. I shall explain this position a little.

Someone finds that a lust brings him into the condition described earlier. It is powerful, strong and riotous; it takes him captive, vexes and disturbs him, and robs him of peace. He cannot bear it, so he sets himself against it, prays against it, groans under it, and sighs to be delivered. But meanwhile, perhaps, in other duties, in constant fellowship with God, in reading, prayer and meditation, in other ways not of the same kind as the lust that troubles him, he is loose and careless. Let that person not think he will ever reach the putting to death of the lust that troubles him. This is a condition that quite often comes on people on their pilgrimage. The Israelites, under a sense of their sin, drew near to God with great diligence and earnestness, with fasting and prayer (Isa. 58). Much is said of their earnestness in the work: “They seek me daily, and delight to know my ways... they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in approaching to God” (verse 2). But God rejects it all. Their fast is a remedy that will not heal them, and the reason given (verses 5–7) is that they were selective in this duty. They attended diligently to that, but were careless and negligent in others. Suppose someone has a “running sore” (that is the Scripture’s expression) arising from an unhealthy state of body brought on by excess and bad diet. Let him apply himself with all the diligence and skill he can to curing the sore; if he leaves the general state of his body diseased, his labour and effort will be in vain. So will be the attempts of someone who tries to stop a bloody flow of sin and filth in his soul and is not equally careful of his whole spiritual health and constitution. For:

(1.) This kind of effort at mortification comes from a corrupt principle, ground and foundation, so it will never come to a good outcome. The true and acceptable principles of mortification will be dwelt on later. Hatred of sin as sin, not only as something that stings or disturbs, and a sense of the love of Christ in the cross, lie at the bottom of all true spiritual mortification. Now, it is certain that what I am speaking of comes from self-love. You set yourself with all diligence and earnestness to put to death a certain lust or sin. Why? It disturbs you; it has taken away your peace; it fills your heart with sorrow, trouble and fear; you have no rest because of it. Yes; but, friend, you have neglected prayer or reading; you have been vain and loose in your conduct in other things that are not of the same nature as the lust that troubles you. These are no less sins and evils than the ones you groan under. Jesus Christ bled for them too. Why do you not set yourself against them as well? If you hated sin as sin, every evil way, you would be no less watchful against everything that grieves and disturbs the Spirit of God than against what grieves and disturbs your own soul. It is clear that you fight against sin merely because of your own trouble from it. If your conscience could be quiet under it, you would leave it alone. If it did not disturb you, it would not be disturbed by you. Now, can you think that God will join in with such hypocritical efforts, that His Spirit will ever bear witness to the treachery and falseness of your spirit? Do you think He will relieve you of what troubles you, so that you may be free for what grieves Him no less? No. God says, “Here is someone who, if he could be rid of this lust, I would never hear from again. Let him wrestle with this, or he is lost.” Let no one think he can do his own work who will not do God’s. God’s work consists in obedience in everything; being freed from the present trouble is only their own. Hence the apostle says, “Let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7:1). If we are to do anything, we must do everything. So what is accepted is not only an intense opposition to this or that particular lust, but a humble state and temper of heart in everything, with watchfulness over every evil and for the performance of every duty.

(2.) How do you know that God has not allowed the lust that has troubled you to gain strength in you and power over you to chasten you for your other neglects and your general lukewarmness in walking before Him; or at least to awaken you to consider your ways, so that you may make a thorough work and change in your course of walking with Him?

The rage and dominance of a particular lust is commonly the fruit and outcome of a careless, negligent life in general, and that for two reasons:

[1.] As its natural effect, if I may put it that way. Lust, as I showed in general, lies in the heart of everyone, even the best, as long as he lives. And do not think that Scripture speaks in vain when it says that lust is subtle, cunning and crafty, that it seduces, entices, fights and rebels. While a person keeps a diligent watch over his heart, its root and fountain, while above all keeping he keeps his heart, from which come the issues of life and death, lust withers and dies in it. But if through negligence it breaks out in some particular direction, gets a passage to the thoughts through the affections, and from them and through them perhaps breaks out into open sin in his conduct, its strength bends the way it has found, and presses mainly that way. Having got a passage, it then vexes and disturbs, and is not easily restrained. In this way a person may be forced to wrestle in sorrow all his days with something that a strict and complete watch might easily have prevented.

[2.] As I said, God often allows it to chasten our other neglects. With wicked people, He gives them up to one sin as the judgment for another, a greater as the punishment for a lesser, or one that will hold them more firmly and securely in place of one they might possibly have been delivered from. So even with His own people He may, and does, sometimes leave them to some troublesome disorders, either to prevent or to cure some other evil. So the messenger of Satan was let loose on Paul, “lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations.” Was it not a correction of Peter’s vain confidence that he was left to deny his Master? Now, if this is the state and condition of lust when it prevails, that God often allows it to prevail to warn us and humble us, perhaps to chasten and correct us for our general loose and careless walk, is it possible that the effect should be removed while the cause continues, that the particular lust should be put to death while the general course is unreformed? Whoever, then, would really, thoroughly and acceptably put to death any disturbing lust, let him take care to be equally diligent in every part of obedience, and know that every lust and every neglect of duty is burdensome to God, even though only one is burdensome to him. While there remains in the heart a treacherous willingness to indulge any negligence, by not pressing on toward full perfection of obedience in everything, the soul is weak, because it does not give faith its whole work; selfish, because it considers the trouble of sin more than its filth and guilt; and lives under a constant provocation of God. So it may not expect any comforting outcome in any spiritual duty it undertakes, much less in this one we are considering, which requires another principle and state of spirit for its accomplishment.

fields.title: Consider the Dangerous Symptoms of Any Lust
fields.body_html:
Particular directions for the case set out above — First: consider the dangerous symptoms of any lust — 1. Long standing — 2. Peace gained in spite of it; the several ways this is done — 3. Frequent success in its seductions — 4. The soul fighting against it only with arguments drawn from the outcome — 5. Its coming with judicial hardness — 6. Its holding out against particular dealings from God — The state of people in whom these things are found.

III. Taking the general rules above for granted, I now come to what I chiefly aim at: particular directions to guide the soul when it is aware of a disturbing lust or disorder. Some of these are preliminary and preparatory, and some contain the work itself. Of the first kind are the following:

First. Consider what dangerous symptoms come with your lust or accompany it, whether or not it has any deadly mark on it. If it does, extraordinary remedies must be used; an ordinary course of mortification will not do.

You will say, “What are these dangerous marks and symptoms, these desperate companions of an indwelling lust, that you mean?” I shall name some of them:

1. Long standing. If it has lain corrupting in your heart for a long time; if you have let it remain in power and dominance for some long time, without vigorously trying to kill it and to heal the wounds you have received from it, your disorder is dangerous. Have you let worldliness, ambition or an excessive appetite for study eat up other duties for a long time, the duties in which you ought to keep up constant fellowship with God? Or have you let impurity defile your heart with vain, foolish and wicked imaginations for many days? Your lust has a dangerous symptom. So it was with David: “My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. 38:5). When a lust has lain long in the heart, corrupting, festering and cankering, it brings the soul into a woeful condition. In such a case an ordinary course of humbling will not do the work. Whatever the lust is, in this way it will work itself more or less into every faculty of the soul, and accustom the affections to its company and fellowship. It grows familiar to the mind and conscience, so that they are not startled by it as by something strange, but make free with it as with something they are used to. Indeed, it will gain such an advantage in this way that it often shows itself and works without being noticed at all, as seems to have been the case with Joseph when he swore by the life of Pharaoh. Unless some extraordinary course is taken, such a person has no ground in the world to expect that his end will be peace.

For, first, how will he be able to tell the difference between the long stay of an unmortified lust and the dominion of sin, which cannot happen to a regenerate person? Secondly, how can he promise himself that it will ever be otherwise with him, or that his lust will ever stop rioting and seducing, when he sees it fixed and staying, as it has for many days, and that it has gone through a variety of conditions with him? Perhaps it has been tried by mercies and afflictions, possibly so remarkable that the soul could not help taking special notice of them. Perhaps it has weathered many a storm, and has sat under a great variety of gifts in the ministry of the word. Will it prove easy to evict a lodger who claims a right by long possession? Old neglected wounds are often fatal and always dangerous. Indwelling disorders grow rusty and stubborn when they are left at ease and in quiet. Lust is a lodger that, if it can claim time and some right of long possession, will not easily be thrown out. As it never dies by itself, so if it is not killed daily it will always gather strength.

2. Secret pleas of the heart to excuse itself and keep up its peace while a lust remains, without a vigorous gospel attempt to put it to death, are another dangerous symptom of a deadly disorder in the heart. Now, there are several ways this may be done. I shall name some of them:

(1.) When, on having thoughts, troubling thoughts, about sin, instead of applying himself to its destruction, a person searches his heart to see what evidence he can find of a good condition in spite of that sin and lust, so that it may still go well with him.

For someone to gather up his experiences of God, to call them to mind, collect them, consider, test and make use of them, is an excellent thing, a duty practised by all the saints and commended in the Old Testament and the New. This was David’s work when he communed with his own heart and called to remembrance the former loving-kindness of the Lord. This is the duty Paul sets us to practise in 2 Cor. 13:5. And as it is excellent in itself, so it has beauty added to it by a fitting season, a time of trial or temptation, or of unrest in the heart about sin; this is a setting of silver for this golden apple, as Solomon puts it. But to do it for this purpose, to satisfy a conscience that is crying and calling for something else, is a desperate device of a heart in love with sin. When a person’s conscience deals with him, when God rebukes him for the sinful disorder of his heart, if instead of applying himself to get that sin pardoned in the blood of Christ and put to death by His Spirit, he relieves himself with whatever other evidences he has, or thinks he has, and so slips out from under the yoke God was putting on his neck, his condition is very dangerous and his wound hard to cure. So the Jews, under the stinging of their own consciences and the convincing preaching of our Saviour, propped themselves up with this: that they were “Abraham’s seed,” and on that account accepted by God. And so they excused themselves in every abominable wickedness, to their utter ruin.

This is, in some degree, a man blessing himself, and saying that on one ground or another he will have peace, “to add drunkenness to thirst.” Love of sin, and a low valuation of peace and of every taste of love from God, are wrapped up in such a state of mind. Such a person plainly shows that, if he can only keep up the hope of escaping “the wrath to come,” he can be quite content to be unfruitful in the world, at any distance from God short of final separation. What can be expected from such a heart?

(2.) This deception is carried on by applying grace and mercy to a sin that is not put to death, or that he is not sincerely trying to put to death. This is a sign of a heart greatly entangled with the love of sin. When someone has secret thoughts in his heart not unlike those of Naaman about his worshipping in the house of Rimmon, “In everything else I will walk with God, but in this one thing may God be merciful to me,” his condition is sad. It is true that a resolution of this kind, to indulge oneself in any sin on the strength of mercy, seems to be, and in any settled course certainly is, wholly inconsistent with Christian sincerity. It is a badge of a hypocrite, and is “turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness.” Yet I have no doubt that, through the craft of Satan and their own remaining unbelief, the children of God may themselves sometimes be caught by this deceit of sin; otherwise Paul would never have warned them against it as he does in Rom. 6:1–2. Indeed, nothing is more natural than for fleshly reasonings to grow high and strong on this ground. The flesh would gladly be indulged on the strength of grace, and it stands ready to catch at every word spoken about mercy and twist it to its own corrupt aims and purposes. To apply mercy, then, to a sin that is not vigorously being put to death is to accomplish the aim of the flesh by means of the gospel.

These and many other ways and tricks a deceitful heart will sometimes use to excuse itself in its abominations. Now, when someone with his sin is in this condition, where a secret liking for the sin prevails in his heart, and though his will is not wholly set on it, he has a half-formed wish toward it, and would practise it if it were not for certain considerations, and so he relieves himself by other means than putting it to death and having it pardoned in the blood of Christ, that person’s “wounds stink and are corrupt,” and without speedy deliverance he will be at death’s door.

3. Frequent success in sin’s seduction, in winning the prevailing consent of the will, is another dangerous symptom. This is what I mean: when the sin in question gets the consent of the will with some delight, even if it is not actually carried out outwardly, it has still had success. A person may be unable, for outward reasons, to go along with sin as far as what James calls its being “finished,” as to the outward acts of sin, when the will to sin has still actually been obtained. Then, I say, it has had success. Now, if any lust can prevail this far in anyone’s soul, then, though his condition may possibly be very bad and he himself unregenerate, it certainly cannot be very good; it is dangerous. And it makes no real difference whether this happens by the choice of the will or by inattention, for that inattention is itself in a way chosen. When we are inattentive and careless where we are bound to be watchful and careful, that inattention does not take away the voluntariness of what we do as a result. For although people do not choose and resolve to be careless and inattentive, if they choose the things that will make them so, they choose inattention itself, as a thing may be chosen in its cause.

And let no one think that the evil of his heart is in any way lessened because he seems for the most part to be taken by surprise into the consent he seems to give it. For it is neglect of his duty of watching over his heart that betrays him into being taken by surprise.

4. When someone fights against his sin only with arguments drawn from its outcome, or the punishment due to it, this is a sign that sin has taken great possession of the will, and that there is an overflow of wickedness in the heart. Someone who sets nothing against the seduction of sin and lust in his heart except fear of shame among people or of hell from God is clearly resolved to do the sin if no punishment went with it. And how that differs from living in the practice of sin, I do not know. Those who are Christ’s, and are moved in their obedience by gospel principles, have the death of Christ, the love of God, the detestable nature of sin, the preciousness of fellowship with God, and a deep-rooted loathing of sin as sin, to set against any seduction of sin and against all the workings, strivings and fightings of lust in their hearts. So it was with Joseph: “How then can I do this great wickedness,” he says, “and sin against God?” my good and gracious God. And Paul: “The love of Christ constraineth us”; and, “Having therefore these promises... let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit” (2 Cor. 7:1). But if someone is so under the power of his lust that he has nothing but law to oppose it with; if he cannot fight against it with gospel weapons, but deals with it entirely with hell and judgment, which are the proper weapons of the law; it is very clear that sin has taken possession of his will and affections to a very great degree of dominance and conquest.

Such a person has thrown off, as far as this particular sin goes, the guidance of renewing grace, and is kept from ruin only by restraining grace. And to that extent he has fallen from grace and returned under the power of the law. And can it be thought that this is not a great provocation to Christ, that people should throw off His easy, gentle yoke and rule, and put themselves under the iron yoke of the law, merely out of indulgence of their lusts?

Test yourself by this as well. When sin drives you to a standstill, so that you must either serve it and rush into folly at its command, like a horse into battle, or make a stand against it to suppress it, what do you say to your soul? How do you argue with yourself? Is this all: “Hell will be the end of this course; vengeance will catch up with me and find me out”? It is time for you to look around you; evil lies at the door. Paul’s main argument to show that sin will not have dominion over believers is that they “are not under the law, but under grace” (Rom. 6:14). If your fighting against sin is all on legal grounds, from legal principles and motives, what assurance can you reach that sin will not have dominion over you, which would be your ruin?

Indeed, know that this reserve will not hold out for long. If your lust has driven you out of stronger gospel forts, it will soon prevail against this one too. Do not suppose that such considerations will deliver you, when you have voluntarily handed over to your enemy those helps and means of preservation that have a thousand times their strength. Be quite sure of this: unless you quickly recover yourself from this condition, the thing you fear will come upon you. What gospel principles do not do, legal motives cannot do.

5. When it is likely that there is, or may be, something of judicial hardening, or at least of chastening punishment, in your lust’s disturbing you. This is another dangerous symptom. I have no doubt that God sometimes leaves even His own people under the troubling power, at least, of some lust or sin, to correct them for earlier sins, neglect and folly. Hence the Church’s complaint: “Why hast thou... hardened our heart from thy fear?” (Isa. 63:17). No one questions that this is His way of dealing with unregenerate people. But how can someone know whether God’s chastening hand has anything to do with his being left to the disturbance of his disorder? Answer. Examine your heart and ways. What was the state and condition of your soul before you fell into the entanglements of the sin you now complain of so much? Had you been careless in duties? Had you lived for yourself without restraint? Is the guilt of some great unrepented sin lying on you? A new sin may be permitted, just as a new affliction may be sent, to bring an old sin to remembrance.

Have you received some outstanding mercy, protection or deliverance that you did not make proper use of, or were not thankful for? Or have you gone through some affliction without working for the purpose it was appointed for? Or have you failed to use the opportunities for glorifying God in your generation that He had graciously given you in His good providence? Or have you conformed yourself to the world and its people, through the abundance of temptations in the days you live in? If you find that this has been your state, wake up and call on God. You are fast asleep in a storm of anger all around you.

6. When your lust has already held out against particular dealings from God against it. This condition is described in Isa. 57:17: “For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth, and smote him: I hid me, and was wroth, and he went on frowardly in the way of his heart.” God had dealt with them about their prevailing lust in several ways, by affliction and by withdrawing Himself; but they held out against everything. This is a sad condition, from which nothing but pure sovereign grace (as God puts it in the next verse) can relieve someone, and which no one ought to promise himself or lean on. God often meets with someone in His providential dealings, and speaks particularly to the evil of his heart, as He did to Joseph’s brothers about their selling him into Egypt. This makes the person reflect on his sin and judge himself in particular for it. God makes it the voice of the danger, affliction, trouble or sickness he is in or under. Sometimes in reading the word God makes a person pause on something that cuts him to the heart and shakes him about his present condition. More often He meets with people in hearing the word preached, His great ordinance for conviction, conversion and building up. God often hews people with the sword of His word in that ordinance. He strikes directly at their bosom-beloved lust, startles the sinner, and makes him commit himself to putting to death and giving up the evil of his heart. Now, if his lust has taken such a hold on him as to force him to break these bands of the Lord and throw off these cords; if it overcomes these convictions and gets back into its old position; if it can heal the wounds it receives like this; that soul is in a sad condition.

The evils that come with such a state of heart are beyond words. Every particular warning to a person in such a condition is a priceless mercy. How, then, does someone who holds out against them despise God in them! And what infinite patience it is in God that He does not cast such a person off and swear in His wrath that he will never enter His rest!

These and many other things are evidence of a lust that is dangerous, if not deadly. As our Saviour said of the evil spirit, “This kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting,” so I say of lusts of this kind. An ordinary course of mortification will not do it; extraordinary means must be settled on.

This is the first particular direction: consider whether the lust or sin you are fighting has any of these dangerous symptoms with it.

Before I go on, I must give you one caution in passing, in case anyone is deceived by what has been said. Though I say the things and evils mentioned above may happen to true believers, let no one who finds the same things in himself conclude from them that he is a true believer. These are evils believers may fall into and be caught by, not the things that make someone a believer. A person might as well conclude that he is a believer because he is an adulterer, since David, who was one, fell into adultery, as conclude it from the signs above, which are the evils of sin and Satan in the hearts of believers. The seventh chapter of Romans describes a regenerate man. Anyone who considers what is said there of his dark side, of his unregenerate part, of the indwelling power and violence of sin remaining in him, and concludes that he is a regenerate man because he finds the same in himself, will be mistaken in his reckoning. It is just as if you argued: a wise man may be sick and wounded, and may even do some foolish things; so everyone who is sick and wounded and does foolish things is a wise man. Or as if a silly, misshapen person, hearing someone say of a beautiful person that he had a mark or scar that disfigured him greatly, should conclude that because he himself has scars and moles and warts, he too is beautiful. If you want evidence that you are a believer, it must come from the things that make people believers. Someone who has these things in him may safely conclude, “If I am a believer, I am a most miserable one.” But to know that anyone is one, he must look for other evidence if he wants peace.

fields.title: Get a Clear Sense of the Guilt, Danger and Evil of the Sin
fields.body_html:
The second particular direction: get a clear sense of — 1. The guilt of the troubling sin — Considerations to help with this — 2. Its many dangers — (1.) Hardening — (2.) Correction in this life — (3.) Loss of peace and strength — (4.) Eternal destruction — Rules for handling this consideration — 3. Its evil — (1.) In grieving the Spirit — (2.) Wounding the new creature — [(3.) Taking away a person’s usefulness.]

The second direction is this: Get a clear and lasting sense on your mind and conscience of the guilt, danger and evil of the sin that troubles you.

1. Of its guilt. One of the deceptions of a prevailing lust is to play down its own guilt. “Is it not a little one?” “When I bow down in the house of Rimmon, may the Lord pardon me in this thing.” “Though this is bad, it is not as bad as such and such an evil. Others of God’s people have been in this state; indeed, what dreadful actual sins some of them have fallen into!” There are countless ways in which sin turns the mind aside from a right and proper grasp of its guilt. Its foul fumes darken the mind, so that it cannot judge things rightly. Confusing reasonings, softening promises, riotous desires, treacherous intentions of giving it up, hopes of mercy: all play their part in disturbing the mind as it considers the guilt of a prevailing lust. The prophet tells us that lust will do this completely when it reaches its height: “Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart” (Hos. 4:11); the heart, that is, the understanding, as the word is often used in Scripture. And as these things accomplish this work fully in unregenerate people, so they do in part in the regenerate too. Solomon tells you of the one who was enticed by the immoral woman that he was “among the simple ones,” “a young man void of understanding” (Prov. 7:7). And where did his folly show? He says in verse 23: “He knoweth not that it is for his life.” He did not consider the guilt of the evil he was caught up in. And the Lord, giving a reason why His dealings with Ephraim had no better effect, gives this account: “Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart” (Hos. 7:11); he had no understanding of his own miserable condition. Would it have been possible for David to lie so long in the guilt of that abominable sin, unless he had countless corrupt reasonings keeping him from taking a clear look at its ugliness and guilt in the mirror of the law? This is why the prophet sent to wake him up, in dealing with him, shut off every loophole and pretext with his parable, so that he might fall fully under a sense of its guilt. This is the natural result of lust in the heart: it darkens the mind so that it will not judge its guilt rightly. And it has many other ways of excusing itself, which I shall not dwell on now.

Let this, then, be the first care of anyone who wants to put sin to death: to fix in his mind a right judgment of its guilt. To this end, take these considerations to help you:

(1.) Though the power of sin is weakened by indwelling grace in those who have it, so that sin will not have dominion over them as it has over others, the guilt of the sin that still remains is made heavier and greater by it. “What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” (Rom. 6:1–2). “How shall we, that are dead?” The emphasis is on the word “we.” How shall we do it, who, as he goes on to describe, have received grace from Christ to the contrary? We, without doubt, are more evil than anyone if we do it. I shall not dwell on the particular aggravations of the sins of such people: how they sin against more love, mercy, grace, help, relief, means and deliverances than others. But let this consideration stay in your mind: there is unimaginably more evil and guilt in the evil of your heart that remains than there would be in the same amount of sin if you had no grace at all. Note:

(2.) As God sees a great deal of beauty and excellence in the desires of His servants’ hearts, more than in the most glorious works of other people, and indeed more than in most of their own outward performances, which have a greater mixture of sin in them than the desires and longings of grace in the heart; so God sees a great deal of evil in the working of lust in their hearts, more even than in the open, notorious acts of wicked people, or in many outward sins the saints may fall into, since more opposition is made against those, and more humbling generally follows them. So Christ, dealing with His declining children, goes to the root with them and sets their profession aside: “I know thy works” (Rev. 3:15); “You are quite a different thing from what you profess, and this makes you abominable.”

So let these and similar considerations lead you to a clear sense of the guilt of your indwelling lust, so that there may be no room in your heart for softening or excusing thoughts, by which sin will gain strength and prevail without your noticing.

2. Consider its danger, which is of many kinds:

(1.) The danger of being hardened by its deceitfulness. The apostle presses this hard on the Hebrews: “Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb. 3:12–13). “Take heed,” he says; “use every means; consider your temptations; watch diligently. There is a treachery, a deceit, in sin that tends to harden your hearts against the fear of God.” The hardening mentioned here is to the uttermost, complete stubbornness. Sin tends toward it, and every disorder and lust will make at least some progress toward it. You who were tender, and used to melt under the word and under afflictions, will grow, as some have profanely put it, “sermon-proof and sickness-proof.” You who used to tremble at the presence of God, at thoughts of death and of appearing before Him, when you had more assurance of His love than you have now, will have a stubbornness of spirit that is not moved by these things. Your soul and your sin will be spoken of and spoken to, and you will not be concerned at all. You will be able to go through duties, praying, hearing and reading, without your heart being in the least affected. Sin will grow a light thing to you; you will pass it by as nothing. This is what it will grow to. And what will be the end of such a condition? Can anything sadder happen to you? Is it not enough to make any heart tremble, to think of being brought into a state where he has light thoughts of sin? Light thoughts of grace, of mercy, of the blood of Christ, of the law, of heaven and hell, all come in at the same time. Take care. This is what your lust is working toward: hardening the heart, searing the conscience, blinding the mind, numbing the affections and deceiving the whole soul.

(2.) The danger of some great correction in this life, which Scripture calls “vengeance,” “judgment” and “punishment” (Ps. 89:30–33). Though God may not cast you off completely for this abomination lying in your heart, He will visit you with the rod. Though He pardons and forgives, He will take vengeance on your inventions. Oh, remember David and all his troubles! Look at him fleeing into the wilderness, and consider the hand of God on him. Is it nothing to you that God should kill your child in anger, ruin your estate in anger, break your bones in anger, let you become a scandal and a disgrace in anger, kill you, destroy you, make you lie down in darkness, in anger? Is it nothing that He should punish, ruin and undo others for your sake? Do not misunderstand me. I do not mean that God always sends all these things on His own in anger; God forbid! But this I do say: when He deals with you like this, and your conscience bears witness with Him about what your provocations have been, you will find His dealings full of bitterness to your soul. If you do not fear these things, I fear you are under hardness.

(3.) Loss of peace and strength all one’s days. To have peace with God, and to have strength to walk before God, is the sum of the great promises of the covenant of grace. In these things is the life of our souls. Without them in some comforting measure, to live is to die. What good will our lives do us if we do not sometimes see the face of God in peace, or if we have no strength to walk with Him? Now, an unmortified lust will certainly rob people’s souls of both. This case is so plain in David that nothing could be clearer. How often he complains that his bones were broken, his soul disturbed, and his wounds grievous on this account! Take other examples: “For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth... I hid me” (Isa. 57:17). What peace, I ask, is there for a soul while God hides Himself, or what strength while He strikes? “I will go and return to my place, till they acknowledge their offence, and seek my face” (Hos. 5:15): “I will leave them and hide My face, and what will become of their peace and strength?” If, then, you have ever enjoyed peace with God, if His terrors have ever made you afraid, if you have ever had strength to walk with Him, or ever mourned in your prayer and been troubled over your weakness, think of this danger hanging over your head. Perhaps in only a little while you will no longer see the face of God in peace. Perhaps by tomorrow you will not be able to pray, read, hear or perform any duty with the least cheerfulness, life or vigour. And possibly you may never see a quiet hour while you live, but carry broken bones around with you, full of pain and terror, all the days of your life. Indeed, perhaps God will shoot His arrows at you and fill you with anguish and unrest, with fears and perplexities; make you a terror and an astonishment to yourself and others; show you hell and wrath every moment; frighten and alarm you with grim thoughts of His hatred; so that your sore runs in the night and your soul refuses comfort, so that you wish for death rather than life, and your soul may even choose strangling. Consider this a little. Though God may not destroy you completely, He might throw you into this condition, in which you will have vivid, living thoughts of your destruction. Accustom your heart to thoughts of this; let it know what the outcome of its state is likely to be. Do not leave this consideration until you have made your soul tremble within you.

(4.) There is the danger of eternal destruction.

To handle this consideration properly, note:

[1.] There is such a connection between continuing in sin and eternal destruction that, though God does resolve to deliver some from continuing in sin so that they may not be destroyed, He will deliver no one from destruction who continues in sin. So while anyone lies under a lasting power of sin, the threats of destruction and everlasting separation from God are to be held out to him. So Heb. 3:12, to which add 10:38. This is the rule of God’s proceeding: if anyone “departs” from Him or “draws back” through unbelief, “my soul shall have no pleasure in him,” that is, His indignation will pursue him to destruction. So too, plainly, Gal. 6:8.

[2.] Someone who is so entangled under the power of any corruption, as described above, can have at that time no clear, prevailing evidence of his share in the covenant, by whose power he might be delivered from fear of destruction. So destruction from the Lord may rightly be a terror to him, and he may, and ought to, look on it as what will be the end of his course and ways. “There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). True; but who will have the comfort of this statement? Who may take it for himself? Those “who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.” But you will say, “Is this not persuading people to unbelief?” I answer, No. There are two judgments a person may make of himself: first, of his person; and secondly, of his ways. It is the judgment of his ways, not of his person, that I am speaking of. Let someone get the best evidence for his person that he can; still, it is his duty to judge that an evil way will end in destruction. Not to do so is atheism. I do not say that in such a condition a person ought to throw away the evidence of his personal share in Christ; but I do say he cannot keep it. There are two kinds of self-condemnation. First, with respect to what one deserves, when the soul concludes that it deserves to be cast out of God’s presence; and this is so far from being a matter of unbelief that it is an effect of faith. Secondly, with respect to the outcome, when the soul concludes that it will be damned. I do not say this is anyone’s duty, nor do I call people to it. But this I say: the soul should consider the end of the way, so that it may be provoked to flee from it. And this is another consideration that ought to stay with such a soul, if it wants to be freed from the entanglement of its lusts.

3. Consider its evils; I mean its present evils. Danger concerns what is to come; evil, what is present. Some of the many evils that come with an unmortified lust may be mentioned:

(1.) It grieves the holy and blessed Spirit, who is given to believers to live in them and stay with them. So the apostle, urging them away from many lusts and sins (Eph. 4:25–29), gives this as the great motive in verse 30: “Grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.” “Do not grieve that Spirit of God,” he says, “from whom you receive so many and such great benefits,” of which he gives one remarkable and all-embracing example: sealing to the day of redemption. He is grieved by it. As a tender and loving friend is grieved at the unkindness of a friend he has done much for, so it is with this tender and loving Spirit, who has chosen our hearts as a home to live in, and to do for us there all that our souls desire. He is grieved by our harbouring His enemies, those He is to destroy, in our hearts with Him. “He doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men” (Lam. 3:33); and shall we grieve Him daily? So He is sometimes said to be “vexed,” and sometimes “grieved at his heart,” to express the deepest sense of our provocation. Now, if there is anything of gracious feeling left in the soul, if it is not completely hardened by the deceitfulness of sin, this consideration will certainly move it. Consider who and what you are; who the Spirit is who is grieved; what He has done for you; what He comes to your soul for; what He has already done in you; and be ashamed. Among those who walk with God, there is no greater motive and spur to holiness in everything, and to keeping their hearts and spirits in all purity and cleanness, than this: that the blessed Spirit, who has undertaken to live in them, is continually considering what they make welcome in their hearts, and rejoices when His temple is kept undefiled. It was a great aggravation of Zimri’s sin that he brought his adulteress into the congregation in the sight of Moses and the others, who were weeping for the sins of the people (Num. 25:6). And is it not a great aggravation of excusing a lust, or letting it stay in the heart, when it is welcomed there (as it must be, if we are believers) under the special eye and gaze of the Holy Ghost, who takes care to keep His tabernacle pure and holy?

(2.) The Lord Jesus Christ is wounded afresh by it. His new creation in the heart is wounded; His love is thwarted; His enemy is gratified. As a complete abandonment of Him through the deceitfulness of sin is to “crucify... the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame,” so every harbouring of the sin He came to destroy wounds and grieves Him.

(3.) It will take away a person’s usefulness in his generation. His works, efforts and labours seldom receive God’s blessing. If he is a preacher, God commonly blights his ministry, so that he labours in the fire and is not honoured with any success or with doing any work for God. And the same may be said of other conditions. The world today is full of poor, withering professing Christians. How few walk in any beauty or glory! How barren and useless they are, for the most part! Among the many reasons that may be given for this sad state, it may rightly be feared that this is not the least effective one: many people harbour spirit-devouring lusts in their bosoms, which lie like worms at the root of their obedience and eat away at it and weaken it day by day. All graces, and all the ways and means by which any graces may be exercised and strengthened, are damaged in this way; and as for success, God blights such people’s undertakings.

This, then, is my second direction, and it concerns the opposition to be made to lust as it dwells settled in the soul. Keep these or similar considerations of its guilt, danger and evil alive on your heart. Meditate much on these things. Make your heart dwell and stay on them. Set your thoughts to these considerations, and do not let them go off or wander from them until they begin to have a powerful influence on your soul, until they make it tremble.

fields.title: Load Your Conscience with the Guilt of the Troubling Disorder
fields.body_html:
The third direction set out: load your conscience with the guilt of the troubling disorder — The ways and means by which this may be done — The fourth direction: an intense desire for deliverance — The fifth: some disorders deeply rooted in people’s natural temperaments — Considerations about such disorders; ways of dealing with them — The sixth direction: the occasions and advantages of sin to be guarded against — The seventh direction: the first stirrings of sin to be vigorously opposed.

This is my third direction:

Load your conscience with its guilt. Do not only consider that it has guilt, but load your conscience with the guilt of its actual outbreaks and disturbances.

To use this rule properly, I shall give some particular directions:

1. Follow God’s method in it: begin with general things, and then come down to particulars.

(1.) Charge your conscience with the guilt that shows in it when measured against the uprightness and holiness of the law. Bring God’s holy law into your conscience, lay your corruption beside it, and pray that you may be moved by it. Consider the holiness, the spiritual nature, the fiery severity, the inwardness and the absoluteness of the law, and see how you can stand before it. Work much, I say, at moving your conscience with the terror of the Lord in the law, and with how right it is that every one of your transgressions should receive its just reward. Perhaps your conscience will invent shifts and evasions to fend off the power of this consideration: for instance, that the condemning power of the law does not apply to you, that you have been set free from it, and the like; and so, though you do not conform to it, you need not be so troubled about it. But:

[1.] Tell your conscience that, while your unmortified lust lies in your heart, it cannot produce any real evidence that you are free from the condemning power of sin. So perhaps the law may make good its claim against you to full dominion, and then you are lost. So it is best to ponder to the uttermost what it has to say.

Certainly, whoever pleads in the most secret reserve of his heart that he is free from the condemning power of the law, so as secretly to excuse himself in giving the slightest allowance to any sin or lust, cannot produce, on gospel grounds, any evidence amounting to tolerable spiritual security that he is truly and properly freed from what he claims to be delivered from.

[2.] Whatever the outcome, the law has a commission from God to seize transgressors wherever it finds them and bring them before His throne, where they must plead for themselves. This is your present case: the law has found you out, and it will bring you before God. If you can plead a pardon, well and good. If not, the law will do its work.

[3.] In any case, this is the proper work of the law: to expose sin in its guilt, to awaken and humble the soul for it, to be a mirror that shows sin in its true colours. And if you refuse to deal with it on this account, it is not through faith, but through the hardness of your heart and the deceitfulness of sin.

This is a door through which too many professing Christians have gone out into open apostasy. They have claimed such a deliverance from the law that they would no longer consult it for guidance and direction, or measure their sin by it. Little by little, without their noticing, this principle has moved from being a notion to influencing their practical understanding, and having taken possession there, it has turned the will and affections loose to every kind of abomination.

By ways such as these, then, I say, persuade your conscience to listen carefully to what the law says to you in the name of the Lord about your lust and corruption. Oh, if your ears are open, it will speak with a voice that will make you tremble, throw you to the ground and fill you with astonishment. If you are ever going to put your corruptions to death, you must tie your conscience to the law and shut it off from every shift and exception, until it owns its guilt with a clear and thorough understanding, so that, as David says, your “sin is ever before” you.

(2.) Bring your lust to the gospel, not for relief, but for further conviction of its guilt. Look on Him whom you have pierced, and be in bitterness. Say to your soul: “What have I done? What love, what mercy, what blood, what grace I have despised and trampled on! Is this how I repay the Father for His love, the Son for His blood, the Holy Ghost for His grace? Is this how I repay the Lord? Have I defiled the heart Christ died to wash, which the blessed Spirit has chosen to live in? And can I keep myself out of the dust? What can I say to the dear Lord Jesus? How can I hold up my head with any boldness before Him? Do I value fellowship with Him so little that, for the sake of this vile lust, I have left Him hardly any room in my heart? How shall I escape if I neglect so great a salvation? Meanwhile, what shall I say to the Lord? Love, mercy, grace, goodness, peace, joy, consolation: I have despised them all and counted them as nothing, so that I might harbour a lust in my heart. Have I been given a sight of God’s fatherly face so that I might look on His face and provoke Him to His face? Was my soul washed so that room might be made for new defilements? Shall I try to defeat the purpose of the death of Christ? Shall I grieve daily that Spirit by whom I am sealed to the day of redemption?” Put this case to your conscience every day. See whether it can stand before this heightening of its guilt. If this does not make it sink in some measure and melt, I fear your case is dangerous.

2. Come down to particulars. As all the benefits of the gospel, such as redemption, justification and the like, are to be considered under the general heading of the gospel, so in particular consider how the love in them has been shown toward your own soul, to heighten the guilt of your corruption. For example:

(1.) Consider the infinite patience and forbearance of God toward you in particular. Consider what advantages He might have taken against you, to make you a shame and a disgrace in this world and an object of wrath for ever. Consider how you have dealt treacherously and falsely with Him time after time, flattering Him with your lips but breaking every promise and commitment, and that through the very sin you are now pursuing. And yet He has spared you time after time, even though you seem boldly to have tested how long He could hold out. And will you still sin against Him? Will you still weary Him, and make Him serve with your corruptions?

Have you not often been ready to conclude that it was utterly impossible for Him to bear with you any longer; that He would cast you off and be gracious no more; that all His forbearance was used up, and hell and wrath were all but prepared for you? And yet, beyond all your expectation, He has come back with visits of love. And will you still go on provoking the eyes of His glory?

(2.) How often have you been at the door of being hardened by the deceitfulness of sin, and by the infinitely rich grace of God been brought back to fellowship with Him again?

Have you not found grace declining; delight in duties, ordinances, prayer and meditation fading away; inclinations to a loose, careless life thriving; and those that were tangled up before almost beyond recovery? Have you not found yourself caught up, and with delight, in ways, associations and company that God loathes? And will you risk going to the brink of hardness again?

(3.) All God’s gracious dealings with you, in providences, deliverances, afflictions, mercies and enjoyments, ought to come in here too. By these, I say, and similar means, load your conscience. Do not let it go until it is thoroughly moved by the guilt of your indwelling corruption, until it feels its wound and lies in the dust before the Lord. Unless this is done in earnest, all other efforts are to no purpose. As long as the conscience has any means of lightening the guilt of sin, the soul will never vigorously attempt to put it to death.

Fourthly. Having been moved in this way by your sin, next get a constant longing and yearning for deliverance from its power. Do not let your heart be content for one moment with its present state and condition. In natural and ordinary matters, longing for anything has no value or importance except as it stirs up the person who has it to a diligent use of means to bring about what he aims at. In spiritual things it is different. Longing, yearning and panting for deliverance is a grace in itself, and has a mighty power to shape the soul into the likeness of what it longs for. So the apostle, describing the repentance and godly sorrow of the Corinthians, counts this as one outstanding grace that was then set to work: “vehement desire” (2 Cor. 7:11). And in this case of indwelling sin and its power, what state does he show himself to be in? Rom. 7:24: his heart bursts out with longing into a most passionate expression of desire for deliverance. Now, if this is the state of the saints when they consider indwelling sin in general, how much more must it be heightened and increased when the troubling rage and power of some particular lust and corruption is added! Be sure of this: unless you long for deliverance, you will not have it.

This will make the heart watchful for every opportunity of gaining an advantage over its enemy, and ready to take hold of any help that is offered for its destruction. Strong desires are the very life of that “praying always” which we are commanded in every condition, and in none is it more necessary than in this. They set faith and hope to work, and are the soul’s moving after the Lord.

So get your heart into a panting, yearning state: long, sigh and cry out. You know David’s example; I need not dwell on it.

The fifth direction is this:

Consider whether the disorder that troubles you is not rooted in your nature, and nourished, fed and heightened by your constitution. No doubt a tendency to some sins may lie in people’s natural temperament and disposition. In this case consider:

1. This is not in the least an excuse that lessens the guilt of your sin. Some, with open profanity, will put gross wickedness down to their temperament and disposition; and whether others may not relieve themselves of the pressing guilt of their disorders by the same reasoning, I do not know. It is from the fall, from the original corruption of our nature, that the tinder and fuel of any sin remain in our natural temperament. David counts his being shapen in iniquity and conceived in sin as an aggravation of the sin that followed, not as something that lessens or excuses it. That you are especially inclined to some sinful disorder is only a particular breaking out of original lust in your nature, which ought to humble and lower you in a particular way.

2. What you need to fix your mind on, in this respect, regarding your walk with God, is that your temperament and disposition give such a great advantage to sin, and to Satan as well, that without extraordinary watchfulness, care and diligence they will certainly prevail against your soul. Thousands have been rushed headlong to hell for this reason, who otherwise might at least have gone at a gentler, less provoking, less damaging pace.

3. For putting to death any disorder rooted like this in a person’s nature, besides all the other ways and means already named or still to be discussed, there is one method especially suited to it. It is the apostle’s: “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor. 9:27). Bringing the very body into subjection is an ordinance of God that tends to the putting to death of sin. It checks the natural root of the disorder and withers it by taking away the richness of its soil. Because the Roman Catholics, people ignorant of the righteousness of Christ, the work of His Spirit and the whole business in hand, have laid the whole weight and stress of mortification on voluntary services and penances aimed at bringing the body under subjection, knowing the true nature neither of sin nor of mortification, this may perhaps be a temptation to some on the other side to neglect certain means of humbling that God Himself owns and has appointed. Bringing the body into subjection in the case in question, by cutting short the natural appetite, by fasting, watching and the like, is without doubt acceptable to God, provided it is done within the following limits:

(1.) The outward weakening and wearing down of the body must not be regarded as good in itself, or as if any mortification consisted in it, for that would bring us back under carnal ordinances. It must be regarded only as a means to the end in view: the weakening of some disorder in its natural root and seat. A person may have leanness of body and of soul together.

(2.) The means by which this is done, namely fasting, watching and the like, must not be regarded as things that in themselves, by their own power, can produce true mortification of any sin. If they could, sin might be put to death without any help from the Spirit in any unregenerate person in the world.
