They are to be regarded only as ways through which the Spirit may, and sometimes does, put out His strength to accomplish His own work, especially in the case mentioned. A lack of right understanding and proper use of these and similar considerations has produced a mortification among the Roman Catholics that would suit horses and other beasts of the field better than believers.

This is the sum of what has been said: when the disorder complained of seems to be rooted in the natural temperament and constitution, then, while applying our souls to share in the blood and Spirit of Christ, we should try to check the natural root of that disorder in God’s way.

The sixth direction is this:

Consider what occasions and advantages your disorder has taken to show itself and break out, and watch against them all.

This is one part of the duty our blessed Saviour commends to His disciples under the name of watching: “What I say unto you I say unto all, Watch” (Mark 13:37), which in Luke 21:34 is, “Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged.” Watch against every outbreak of your corruptions. I mean the duty David professed to be exercised in: “I kept myself from mine iniquity,” he says. He watched all the ways and workings of his iniquity, to forestall them and to rise up against them. This is what we are called to under the name of “considering our ways.” Consider what ways, what company, what opportunities, what studies, what business and what conditions have at any time given, or usually give, advantages to your disorders, and set yourself carefully against them all. People will do this with their bodily weaknesses and illnesses. The seasons, the diet and the air that have proved harmful will be avoided. Are the things of the soul less important? Know that whoever dares to toy with occasions of sin will dare to sin. Whoever will venture into temptations to wickedness will venture into wickedness. Hazael thought he would not be as wicked as the prophet told him he would be. To convince him, the prophet told him no more than, “Thou shalt be king over Syria.” If he would venture into temptations to cruelty, he would be cruel. Tell someone he will commit such and such sins, and he will be startled. If you can convince him that he will venture into the occasions and temptations of them, he will have little ground left for his confidence. There are many particular directions under this heading, not to be dwelt on now. But because this heading is as important as the whole doctrine dealt with here, I have treated it at length in another treatise, on entering into temptation.

The seventh direction is this:

Rise up mightily against the first stirrings of your disorder, its first conceptions. Do not let it gain the least ground. Do not say, “It shall go this far and no further.” If it is allowed one step, it will take another. It is impossible to set limits to sin. It is like water in a channel: once it breaks out, it will run its course. It is easier to keep it from acting at all than to keep it within bounds. That is why James sets out the stages and progress of lust (James 1:14–15), so that we may stop it at the entrance. Do you find your corruption beginning to entangle your thoughts? Rise up with all your strength against it, with no less indignation than if it had fully accomplished what it aims at. Consider what an unclean thought would have: it would have you roll yourself in folly and filth. Ask envy what it would have: murder and destruction lie at the end of it. Set yourself against it with no less vigour than if it had utterly debased you to wickedness. Without this course you will not prevail. As sin gains ground in the affections, so that they delight in it, it also gains ground on the understanding, so that it thinks lightly of it.

fields.title: Thinking on the Excellence of God’s Majesty
fields.body_html:
The eighth direction: thinking much on the excellence of God’s majesty — How little we really know Him, set out and considered.

Eighthly, train and exercise yourself in meditations that may serve to fill you at all times with humility and thoughts of your own vileness, such as these:

1. Think much on the excellence of God’s majesty and your infinite, unimaginable distance from Him. Thinking of this often is bound to fill you with a sense of your own vileness, which strikes deep at the root of any indwelling sin. When Job comes to a clear sight of the greatness and excellence of God, he is filled with self-loathing and pressed down into humility (Job 42:5–6). And what state does the prophet Habakkuk say he was thrown into when he grasped the majesty of God (Hab. 3:16)? “With God,” says Job, “is terrible majesty.” Hence the belief of people of old that, once they had seen God, they would die. Scripture is full of this humbling consideration, comparing the people of the earth to “grasshoppers,” to “vanity,” to “the small dust of the balance,” compared with God. Think much along these lines, to humble the pride of your heart and keep your soul lowly within you. Nothing will make you less open to being taken in by the deceptions of sin than a heart in this state. Think greatly of the greatness of God.

2. Think much about how little you really know Him. Though you know enough to keep you low and humble, how small a portion of Him you know! Contemplating this threw that wise man into the view of himself that he expresses in Prov. 30:2–4: “Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man. I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy. Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell?” Work at this too, to bring down the pride of your heart. What do you know of God? How small a portion it is! How immense He is in His nature! Can you look into the abyss of eternity without terror? You cannot bear the rays of His glorious being.

Because I regard this consideration as very useful in our walk with God, as far as it is consistent with the childlike boldness given us in Jesus Christ to draw near to the throne of grace, I shall dwell on it further, to leave a lasting impression of it on the souls of those who want to walk humbly with God.

Consider, then, I say, so as to keep your heart in continual awe of God’s majesty, that even people of the highest and most eminent attainments, who have the nearest and most familiar fellowship with God, still know very little of Him and His glory in this life. God revealed His name to Moses, the most glorious attributes He has shown in the covenant of grace (Exod. 34:5–6); yet all of it was only the “back parts” of God. All Moses knew by it was little and lowly compared with the perfections of His glory. That is why it is said, with special reference to Moses, “No man hath seen God at any time” (John 1:18). He is speaking of Moses in comparison with Christ in verse 17, and of him it is said here that “no man,” not even Moses, the most eminent of them, “hath seen God at any time.” We speak much of God; we can talk of Him, His ways, His works and His counsels all day long. The truth is that we know very little of Him. Our thoughts, meditations and expressions about Him are lowly; many of them are unworthy of His glory, and none of them reaches His perfections.

You will say that Moses lived under the law, when God wrapped Himself in darkness and His mind in types, clouds and dark institutions. Under the glorious shining of the gospel, which has brought life and immortality to light, with God revealed from His own bosom, we now know Him much more clearly, and as He is. We see His face now, and not only His back parts, as Moses did.

Answer. 1. I acknowledge a vast and almost unimaginable difference between the acquaintance we now have with God, since He has spoken to us by His own Son, and that which most of the saints had under the law. Their eyes were as good, sharp and clear as ours; their faith and spiritual understanding were not behind ours; the object was as glorious to them as to us. Yet our day is clearer than theirs was. The clouds have blown away and scattered, the shadows of the night have gone and fled, the sun has risen, and the means of sight have been made more eminent and clear than before. Yet:

2. That special sight Moses had of God in Exodus 34 was a gospel sight, a sight of God as “gracious” and so on; and yet it is called only His “back parts,” that is, low and poor compared with His excellencies and perfections.

3. The apostle, exalting to the uttermost this glory of light above that of the law, and showing that now the “vail” that caused darkness is taken away, so that “we all, with open face beholding... the glory of the Lord,” tells us how: “as in a glass” (2 Cor. 3:18). “In a glass”: how is that? Clearly, perfectly? Alas, no! He tells you how it is in 1 Cor. 13:12: “For now we see through a glass, darkly.” It is not a telescope he is speaking of, which helps us to see things far away; and even so, what poor helps telescopes are! How far short of the truth of things we fall in spite of their help! It is a mirror he alludes to, where there are only dim reflections and images of things and not the things themselves, and he compares our knowledge to the sight we have in it. He also tells you that all we do see δι’ ἐσόπτρου, “by” or “through this glass,” is ἐν αἰνίγματι, “in a riddle,” in darkness and obscurity. And speaking of himself, who was surely far more clear-sighted than anyone now living, he tells us that he saw only ἐκ μέρους, “in part.” He saw only the back parts of heavenly things (verse 12), and he compares all the knowledge of God he had reached to the knowledge he had of things when he was a child (verse 11). It is a μέρος, a part, short of τὸ τέλειον, that which is perfect; indeed, it is such as καταργηθήσεται, “shall be done away.” We know what weak, feeble, uncertain ideas and notions children have of anything difficult to grasp, and how, when they grow up and their abilities develop, those ideas vanish and they are ashamed of them. It is to a child’s credit to love, honour, believe and obey his father; but as for his learning and notions, his father knows how childish and foolish they are. For all our confidence in our high attainments, all our ideas of God are only childish compared with His infinite perfections. For the most part we lisp and babble and say we know not what, even in what we think are our most accurate ideas and notions of God. We may love, honour, believe and obey our Father, and with that He accepts our childish thoughts, for childish they are. We see only His back parts; we know only a little of Him. Hence that promise by which we are so often held up and comforted in our distress: “We shall see him as he is”; we shall see Him “face to face”; we shall “know even as also I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12; 1 John 3:2); and, put plainly, “now we see him not.” All these conclude that here we see only His back parts: not as He is, but in a dark, obscure representation, not in the perfection of His glory.

The queen of Sheba had heard a great deal about Solomon, and had formed many great ideas of his magnificence in her mind as a result. But when she came and saw his glory, she had to confess that she had not been told the half of it. We may suppose that we have reached great knowledge here, and clear and lofty thoughts of God. But, alas, when He brings us into His presence we shall cry out, “We never knew Him as He is. Not a thousandth part of His glory, perfection and blessedness ever entered our hearts.”

The apostle tells us in 1 John 3:2 that we do not know what we ourselves shall be, what we shall find ourselves to be in the end. Much less will it enter our hearts to imagine what God is, and what we shall find Him to be. Consider either the One who is to be known, or the way by which we know Him, and this will appear further:

(1.) We know so little of God because it is God who is to be known: the One who has described Himself to us largely by this very thing, that we cannot know Him. What else does He mean when He calls Himself invisible, incomprehensible and the like, except that He is One whom we do not and cannot know as He is? And our further progress consists more in knowing what He is not than what He is. So He is described as immortal and infinite; that is, He is not mortal, finite and limited, as we are. Hence that glorious description of Him in 1 Tim. 6:16: “Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see.” His light is such that no creature can approach it. He is not seen, not because He cannot be seen, but because we cannot bear the sight of Him. The light of God, in whom is no darkness, forbids all approach to Him by any creature whatever. We who cannot look at the sun in its glory are too weak to bear the beams of infinite brightness. On this consideration, as was said, the wise man confesses himself “more brutish than any man,” without “the understanding of a man” (Prov. 30:2); that is, he knew nothing in comparison with God, so that he seemed to have lost all his understanding once he came to consider God, His work and His ways.

In this consideration, let our souls come down to some particulars:

[1.] As for the being of God, we are so far from knowing it, in a way that would let us teach one another about it in words and expressions, that to form any idea of it in our minds, using the kind of images and impressions by which we gain knowledge of everything else, is to make an idol for ourselves, and so to worship a god of our own making and not the God who made us. We might as well, and as lawfully, carve Him out of wood or stone as form a being for Him in our minds suited to our understanding. The utmost of the best of our thoughts about the being of God is that we can have no thoughts of it. Our knowledge of a being is low indeed when it rises no higher than knowing that we do not know it.

[2.] There are some things about God that He Himself has taught us to speak of, and has governed how we express them. But when we have done so, we do not see the things themselves; we do not know them. To believe and wonder is all we can reach. We profess, as we are taught, that God is infinite, almighty and eternal; and we know what disputes and ideas there are about His being present everywhere, His immensity, infinity and eternity. We have, I say, words and ideas about these things. But as for the things themselves, what do we know? What do we grasp of them? Can the human mind do any more than swallow itself up in an infinite abyss, which is to it as nothing, and give itself up to what it cannot conceive, much less express? Is not our understanding “brutish” in contemplating such things, as if it did not exist? Indeed, the perfection of our understanding is not to understand, and to rest there. We have only a glimpse of the back parts of eternity and infinity. What shall I say of the Trinity, of the existence of distinct persons in the same single essence, a mystery many deny because no one understands it, a mystery of which every letter is mysterious? Who can declare the begetting of the Son, the proceeding of the Spirit, or the difference between the one and the other? But I shall not give further particular examples. The infinite and unimaginable distance between Him and us keeps us in the dark as to any sight of His face or clear grasp of His perfections.

We know Him by what He does rather than by what He is, by His doing us good rather than by His essential goodness. And how small a portion of Him, as Job says, is revealed by this!

(2.) We know little of God because it is by faith alone that we know Him here. I shall not now discuss the remaining impressions on all human hearts by nature that there is a God, nor what people may reasonably be taught about that God from the works of His creation and providence that they see and observe. Admittedly, and on the woeful experience of every age, this knowledge is so weak, low, dark and confused that no one has ever glorified God as they ought because of it. For all their knowledge of God, they were in fact “without God in the world.”

The chief, and in effect almost the only, acquaintance we have with God and His dealings is by faith. “He that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb. 11:6). Our knowledge of Him and of His rewarding, which is the basis of our obedience or coming to Him, is believing. “We walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:7): Διὰ πίστεως οὐ διὰ εἴδους, by faith, and so by faith that we have no distinct idea, image or appearance of what we believe. Faith is all the evidence we have of “things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). I might dwell here on its nature, and show from everything that goes with it and concerns it that we know only the back parts of what we know by faith alone. As to its origin, it is built purely on the testimony of One we have not seen. As the apostle puts it, how can you love Him whom you have not seen? That is, whom you know only by faith that He is. Faith receives everything on His testimony, and receives that He is only on His own testimony. As to its nature, it is assent on the basis of testimony, not evidence on the basis of proof; and its object, as was said before, is above us. So our faith, as was noted earlier, is called seeing “through a glass, darkly.” All we know in this way (and all we know of God we know in this way) is low, dark and obscure.

But you will say: “All this is true, but perhaps only for those who do not know God as He is revealed in Jesus Christ. For those who do, it is different. It is true that ‘no man hath seen God at any time,’ but ‘the only begotten Son... he hath declared him’ (John 1:18); and ‘the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true’ (1 John 5:20). The light of ‘the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God,’ shines on believers (2 Cor. 4:4). Indeed, ‘God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ’ (verse 6). So though we ‘were sometimes darkness,’ we are now ‘light in the Lord’ (Eph. 5:8). And the apostle says, ‘We all, with open face beholding... the glory of the Lord’ (2 Cor. 3:18). We are now so far from being in such darkness, or at such a distance from God, that ‘our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son’ (1 John 1:3). The light of the gospel by which God is now revealed is glorious. Not a star but the sun in its beauty has risen on us, and the veil is taken from our faces. So though unbelievers, and perhaps some weak believers, may be in some darkness, those of any growth or considerable attainment have a clear sight and view of the face of God in Jesus Christ.”

To this I answer:

[1.] The truth is that we all know enough of Him to love Him more than we do, and to delight in Him and serve Him, believe Him, obey Him and trust in Him beyond anything we have reached so far. Our darkness and weakness are no excuse for our negligence and disobedience. Who has ever lived up to the knowledge he has had of God’s perfections, excellencies and will? God’s purpose in giving us any knowledge of Himself here is that we may “glorify him as God,” that is, love Him, serve Him, believe and obey Him, and give Him all the honour and glory due from poor sinful creatures to a sin-pardoning God and Creator. We must all acknowledge that we were never thoroughly transformed into the image of the knowledge we have had. And if we had used our talents well, we might have been trusted with more.

[2.] By comparison, the knowledge we have of God through the revelation of Jesus Christ in the gospel is exceedingly eminent and glorious. It is so in comparison with any knowledge of God that might be gained otherwise, or that was given in the law under the Old Testament, which had only a shadow of good things, not their very image. The apostle pursues this at length in 2 Corinthians 3. In these last days Christ has revealed the Father from His own bosom, declared His name, and made known His mind, will and counsel far more clearly, eminently and distinctly than He did before, while He kept His people under the schoolmaster of the law. And this, for the most part, is what is meant in the passages mentioned above. The clear, plain presentation and declaration of God and His will in the gospel is expressly exalted in comparison with any other way He has revealed Himself.

[3.] The difference between believers and unbelievers in knowledge lies not so much in what they know as in how they know it. Some unbelievers may know more, and be able to say more, about God, His perfections and His will than many believers. But they know nothing as they ought; nothing in the right way; nothing spiritually and savingly; nothing with a holy, heavenly light. The excellence of a believer is not that he has a wide grasp of things, but that whatever he does grasp, which may perhaps be very little, he sees in the light of the Spirit of God, in a saving, soul-transforming light. And this is what gives us fellowship with God, not prying thoughts or ideas raised by curiosity.

[4.] Jesus Christ, by His word and Spirit, reveals God to the hearts of all His people as a Father, as a God in covenant, as a rewarder, in every way sufficient to teach us to obey Him here, and to lead us to His bosom, to lie down there in the enjoyment of Him for eternity. But still:

[5.] In spite of all this, we know only a little portion of Him; we see only His back parts. For:

1st. The purpose of all gospel revelation is not to unveil God’s essential glory, so that we should see Him as He is, but only to declare as much of Him as He knows is enough to be a foundation for our faith, love, obedience and coming to Him; that is, for the faith He expects from us here, and for such service as befits poor creatures in the midst of temptations. But when He calls us to eternal, uninterrupted wonder and contemplation, He will reveal Himself in a new way, and the whole shape of things as it now lies before us will pass away like a shadow.

2dly. We are dull and slow of heart to take in the things revealed in the word. By our weakness and frailty God keeps us continually dependent on Him for teaching and for revelations of Himself from His word, and in this world He never brings any soul to the uttermost of what can be drawn out and discovered from the word. So, although the way of revelation in the gospel is clear and evident, we still know little of the things themselves that are revealed.

Let us, then, return to the use and purpose of this consideration. Will not a proper grasp of this unimaginable greatness of God, and of the infinite distance at which we stand from Him, fill the soul with a holy and reverent fear of Him, and so keep it in a state unsuited to the thriving or flourishing of any lust whatever? Let the soul be continually accustomed to reverent thoughts of God’s greatness and of His presence everywhere, and it will be much on its guard against any improper behaviour. Consider the One you have to deal with: “our God is a consuming fire.” And in your deepest shame at His presence and His eye, know that your very nature is too narrow to bear thoughts that match His essential glory.

fields.title: When the Heart Is Disturbed by Sin, Speak No Peace to It until God Speaks It
fields.body_html:
The ninth direction: when the heart is disturbed by sin, speak no peace to it until God speaks it — Peace without loathing of sin is unsound, and so is peace measured out to ourselves — How we may know when we measure out peace to ourselves — Directions for that inquiry — The emptiness of speaking peace lightly, and of doing it on one account only and not in everything.

Ninthly, if God disturbs the heart about the guilt of its disorders, either as to their root and dwelling in it or as to any outbreaks of them, take care not to speak peace to yourself before God speaks it; but listen to what He says to your soul. This is our next direction, and without keeping it the heart will be greatly exposed to the deceitfulness of sin.

This is a matter of great importance. It is a sad thing for anyone to deceive his own soul here. All the warnings God gives us, out of tenderness for our souls, to test and examine ourselves, aim at preventing this great evil of speaking peace to ourselves without grounds, which in the end is to bless ourselves in opposition to God. My business is not to dwell on its danger, but to help believers prevent it, and to let them know when they are doing it.

To handle this direction rightly, note:

1. It is God’s great prerogative and sovereignty to give grace to whom He pleases (“He hath mercy on whom he will have mercy,” Rom. 9:18; and among all the children of men He calls whom He will and sanctifies whom He will). In the same way, among those who are called and justified and whom He will save, He still keeps this privilege for Himself: to speak peace to whom He pleases, and in what degree He pleases, even among those on whom He has bestowed grace. He is the “God of all comfort” in a special way in His dealings with believers; that is, the God of the good things He keeps locked up in His household and gives out of it to all His children as He pleases. The Lord insists on this in Isa. 57:16–18, and it is the very case we are considering that is dealt with there. When God says He will heal their breaches and their sorrows, He claims this privilege for Himself in a special way: “I create” it (verse 19). “Even with regard to these poor wounded creatures, I create it, and in My sovereignty I give it out as I please.”

So, just as with the giving of grace to those who are in the state of nature, God does it with great care, and His proceedings in taking and leaving people are often, as far as outward appearances go, quite apart from and contrary to every likely expectation; so it is with His giving of peace and joy to those in the state of grace. He often gives them out quite apart from our expectations, as far as any visible grounds for His dealings go.

2. As God creates it for whom He pleases, so it is Christ’s prerogative to speak it home to the conscience. Speaking to the church of Laodicea, which had healed her wounds falsely and spoke peace to herself when she ought not to, He takes this title for Himself: “These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Rev. 3:14). He bears witness to our condition as it really is. We may possibly be mistaken and trouble ourselves for nothing, or flatter ourselves on false grounds; but He is “the Amen, the faithful... witness,” and what He says of our state and condition is what it really is. In Isa. 11:3 He is said not to “judge after the sight of his eyes,” not by any outward appearance, or by anything open to mistake, as we tend to do; but He will judge and decide every case as it really is.

With these two preliminary observations, I shall give some rules by which people may know whether God is speaking peace to them, or whether they are only speaking peace to themselves:

1. People are certainly speaking peace to themselves when it does not come with the deepest loathing imaginable of the sin they are speaking peace about, and with loathing of themselves for it. When people are wounded by sin, disturbed and troubled, and knowing there is no remedy for them except in the mercies of God through the blood of Christ, they look to Him and to the promises of the covenant in Him, and so quiet their hearts that it will be well with them and that God will be exalted so that He may be gracious to them; and yet their souls are not brought to the deepest loathing of the sin or sins that disturb them; this is healing themselves, not being healed by God. It is only a great and strong wind, which the Lord is near, but the Lord is not in the wind. When people truly “look upon me whom they have pierced,” without which there is no healing or peace, they will “mourn” (Zech. 12:10). They will mourn for Him, and for this very reason, and will loathe the sin that pierced Him. When we go to Christ for healing, faith looks on Him especially as one pierced. Faith takes different views of Christ according to the occasions it has for approaching Him and having fellowship with Him. Sometimes it looks at His holiness, sometimes at His power, sometimes at His love, sometimes at His favour with His Father. And when it goes for healing and peace, it looks especially at the blood of the covenant, at His sufferings; for “the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa. 53:5). When we look for healing, His stripes are what we must look at, not in the outward story of them, which is the way of Roman Catholic devotees, but in the love, kindness, mystery and purpose of the cross. And when we look for peace, His chastisement must be before our eyes. Now this, I say, if it is done according to the mind of God and in the strength of the Spirit poured out on believers, will produce a loathing of the sin or sins for which healing and peace are sought. So in Ezek. 16:60–61: “Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with thee in the days of thy youth, and I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant.” And what then? “Then thou shalt remember thy ways, and be ashamed.” When God comes home to speak peace in a sure covenant of it, it fills the soul with shame for all the ways in which it has been estranged from Him. And one of the things the apostle mentions as coming with that godly sorrow which goes with repentance unto salvation, never to be repented of, is revenge: “Yea, what revenge!” (2 Cor. 7:11). They looked back on their failings with indignation and revenge for their folly in them. When Job comes to a thorough healing, he cries, “Wherefore I abhor myself” (Job 42:6); and until he did, he had no lasting peace. He might perhaps have patched himself up with the doctrine of free grace so excellently preached by Elihu in chapter 33, from verse 14 to 30; but then he would only have skinned over his wounds. He must come to self-loathing if he is to come to healing. So it was with those in Ps. 78:33–35, in their great trouble and distress for and because of sin. I have no doubt that, when they approached God in Christ (and it is clear that they did, from the titles they gave Him: they call Him their Rock and their Redeemer, two words that everywhere point to the Lord Christ), they spoke peace to themselves. But was it sound and lasting? No; it passed away like the early dew. God did not speak one word of peace to their souls. But why did they not have peace? Because in approaching God they flattered Him. But how is that clear? Verse 37: “For their heart was not right with him, neither were they stedfast.” They had neither loathing for nor abandonment of the sin they spoke peace to themselves about. Let someone apply for healing and peace however he likes; let him apply to the true Physician; let him do it the right way; let him quiet his heart with the promises of the covenant. Yet when peace is spoken, if it does not come with loathing and hatred of the sin that was the wound and caused the unrest, this is no peace of God’s creating, but of our own procuring. It is only skinning over the wound while the core lies at the bottom, which will rot and corrupt and eat away until it breaks out again with foulness, vexation and danger. Let poor souls who walk this path, who feel the trouble of sin more than the defilement that comes with it, who go for mercy, yes, go to the Lord in Christ for mercy, but still keep the sweet morsel of their sin under their tongue; let them, I say, never think they will have true and solid peace. For example: you find your heart running after the world, and it disturbs you in your fellowship with God. The Spirit says to you expressly, “If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” This sets you dealing with God in Christ for the healing of your soul and the quieting of your conscience. Yet, for all that, a thorough loathing of the evil itself does not stay on you; perhaps you like it well enough, except for its consequences. Perhaps you may be saved, yet as through fire, and God will have some work with you before He is done; but you will have little peace in this life. You will be sick and fainting all your days (Isa. 57:17). This is a deception that lies at the root of the peace of many professing Christians and wastes it away. They deal with all their strength about mercy and pardon, and seem to have great fellowship with God in doing so. They lie before Him and lament their sins and follies, so that anyone would think, and they themselves think, that surely they and their sins have now parted. And so they receive a mercy that satisfies their hearts for a little while. But when a thorough search is made, there has been some secret reserve for the folly or follies in question, or at least there has not been the thorough loathing of it that is necessary. And their whole peace is soon found to be weak and rotten, hardly lasting longer than the words of begging for it are in their mouths.

2. When people measure out peace to themselves on the strength of the conclusions their convictions and reasoning lead them to, this is a false peace and will not last. I shall explain a little what I mean. Someone has been wounded by sin. He has a conviction of some sin on his conscience. He has not walked uprightly as befits the gospel; all is not well and right between God and his soul. He now considers what to do. He has light, and knows what path he must take and how his soul has been healed before. Considering that the promises of God are the outward means to apply for healing his sores and quieting his heart, he goes to them, searches them out, and finds one or more whose wording directly suits his condition. He says to himself, “God speaks in this promise. Here I will take a bandage as long and broad as my wound.” And so he brings the word of the promise to his condition and sits down in peace. This is another appearance on the mountain: the Lord is near, but the Lord is not in it. It has not been the work of the Spirit, who alone can “reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment,” but merely the working of the intelligent, reasoning soul. We say there are three kinds of life: vegetative, sensitive, and rational or intelligent. Some things have only the vegetative; some have the sensitive as well, which includes the first; some have the rational, which takes in and presupposes both the others. Now, whatever has the rational life acts not only in keeping with that principle but also in keeping with both the others: it grows and it senses. It is the same with people in the things of God. Some are merely natural, reasoning people; some have an added conviction, with enlightenment; and some are truly regenerate. Now, whoever has the last has both the others too, and so he sometimes acts on the principles of the reasoning person and sometimes on those of the enlightened person. His true spiritual life is not the source of all his movements; he does not always act in its strength, and not all his fruits come from that root. In the case I am speaking of, he acts merely on the principle of conviction and enlightenment, by which his natural faculties are heightened, but the Spirit does not breathe on these waters at all. Take an example. Suppose the wound and unrest of the soul is because of relapses. Whatever the evil or folly may be, however small in substance, no wounds are deeper than those given the soul for this reason, and no unrest is greater. In the turmoil of his mind he finds the promise in Isa. 55:7, “Let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon,” that is, He will multiply and add to pardon, He will do it again and again; or the one in Hos. 14:4, “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.” The man considers this, and on that basis concludes peace for himself. Whether the Spirit of God makes the application or not, whether He gives life and power to the letter or not, he does not consider. He does not listen to whether God the Lord speaks peace. He does not wait on God, who perhaps is still hiding His face, and sees the poor creature stealing peace and running off with it, knowing the time will come when He will deal with him again and call him to a new reckoning, when he will see that it is useless to go one step where God does not take him by the hand.

I see, indeed, several other questions arising here and pushing themselves in. I cannot address them all, but I shall say a little about one.

It may be said, then: “Since this seems to be the path the Holy Spirit leads us in for the healing of our wounds and the quieting of our hearts, how shall we know when we are going alone, and when the Spirit is going with us?”

Answer. (1.) If any of you are off the path in this, God will soon let you know. For besides having His promise that “the meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way” (Ps. 25:9), He will not let you go on erring for ever. He will not, I say, let your nakedness be covered with fig leaves, but will take them away, and all the peace you have in them, and will not let you settle on such dregs. You will soon know that your wound is not healed; that is, you will soon find out from the outcome whether this is how things are with you. The peace you get and obtain in this way will not last. While the mind is overpowered by its own convictions, there is nothing for unrest to fasten on. Wait a little, and all these reasonings will grow cold and vanish before the first temptation that arises. But:

(2.) This course is usually taken without waiting, which is the grace, and the special working of faith, that God calls for in such a condition. I know God sometimes comes into the soul at once, in a moment as it were, wounding and healing it, as I am persuaded He did in David’s case when he cut off the corner of Saul’s robe. But ordinarily in such a case God calls for waiting and labouring, watching as the eyes of a servant watch his master. The prophet Isaiah says, “I will wait upon the Lord, that hideth his face from the house of Jacob” (Isa. 8:17). When His children have run away from His house, God will have them lie at His door a while, and not rush in on Him at once, unless He takes them by the hand and pulls them in, when they are so ashamed that they dare not come to Him. Now, self-healers, people who speak peace to themselves, usually make haste. They will not wait. They do not listen to what God says, but on they go to be healed.

(3.) Though such a course may quiet the conscience and the mind, the reasoning, concluding part of the soul, it does not sweeten the heart with rest and gracious contentment. The answer it receives is much like the one Elisha gave Naaman: “Go in peace.” It quieted his mind, but I very much doubt whether it sweetened his heart, or gave him any joy in believing beyond the natural joy that was stirred in him by his healing. “Do not my words do good?” says the Lord (Micah 2:7). When God speaks, there is not only truth in His words to answer the conviction of our understanding, but they also do good. They bring what is sweet and good and desirable to the will and affections. By them the soul returns to its rest (Ps. 116:7).

(4.) Worst of all, it does not change the life. It does not heal the evil or cure the disorder. When God speaks peace, He guides and keeps the soul so that it does not “turn again to folly.” When we speak it ourselves, the heart is not drawn away from the evil. Indeed, it is the readiest course in the world for bringing a soul into a habit of backsliding. If, after bandaging yourself, you find yourself more ready for the battle again than completely weaned from it, it is all too plain that you have been at work on your own soul, but Jesus Christ and His Spirit were not there. And often nature, having done its work, will come for its reward before a few days are over, and having been active in the work of healing, will be ready to argue for a new wounding. When God speaks peace, so much sweetness comes with it, and such a revelation of His love, that it lays a strong obligation on the soul never again to act perversely.

3. We speak peace to ourselves when we do it lightly. The prophet complains of this in some teachers: “They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly” (Jer. 6:14). And so it is with some people. They make the healing of their wounds a light matter. A look, a glance of faith at the promises does it, and the matter is closed. The apostle tells us that “the word preached did not profit them,” because it was “not being mixed with faith” (Heb. 4:2): μὴ συγκεκραμένος, “not well blended” and mingled with faith. It is not a mere look at the word of mercy in the promise; it must be mingled with faith until it is incorporated into its very nature, and then indeed it does the soul good. If you have had a wound on your conscience, with weakness and unrest, and are now free of it, how did you get free? “I looked to the promises of pardon and healing, and so found peace.” Yes, but perhaps you were too hasty; you did it superficially. You did not feed on the promise so as to mix it with faith and get all its power spread through your soul; you only did it lightly. You will find your wound breaking out again before long, and you will know that you are not cured.

4. Whoever speaks peace to himself about one thing, while at the same time another evil of no less importance lies on his spirit about which he has had no dealings with God, cries “Peace” when there is none. To explain my meaning a little: someone has neglected a duty again and again, perhaps, when in all righteousness he owed it. His conscience is troubled, his soul is wounded, and he has no quiet in his bones because of his sin. He applies for healing and finds peace. Yet meanwhile, perhaps, worldliness or pride or some other folly that greatly grieves the Spirit of God may lie in that person’s bosom, and they do not disturb him, nor he them. Let that person not think that any of his peace is from God. It will be well with people when they have equal regard for all God’s commandments. God will justify us from our sins, but He will not justify the least sin in us: “Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil.”

5. When people speak peace to their consciences by themselves, God seldom speaks humility to their souls. God’s peace is humbling peace, melting peace, as it was in David’s case. He was never so deeply humbled as when Nathan brought him the news of his pardon.

But you will say, “When may we take the comfort of a promise as our own, with regard to some particular wound, for quieting the heart?”

First, in general: when God speaks it, whenever that may be, sooner or later. I told you before that He may do it at the very moment of the sin itself, and with such irresistible power that the soul cannot help receiving His mind in it. Sometimes He will make us wait longer. But when He speaks, whether sooner or later, whether while we are sinning or repenting, whatever the condition of our souls may be, if God speaks, He must be received. There is nothing in our fellowship with Him that troubles the Lord more about us, if I may put it that way, than our unbelieving fears, which keep us from receiving the strong consolation He is so willing to give us.

But you will say, “We are back where we started. When God speaks it, we must receive it; that is true. But how shall we know when He speaks?”

(1.) I wish we could all come up to this in practice: to receive peace when we are convinced that God speaks it and that it is our duty to receive it. But:

(2.) There is, if I may put it so, a secret instinct in faith by which it knows the voice of Christ when He really speaks. As the baby leaped in the womb when the blessed Virgin came to Elisabeth, so faith leaps in the heart when Christ really draws near to it. “My sheep,” says Christ, “know my voice” (John 10:4). “They know My voice; they are used to its sound.” And they know when His lips are opened to them and are full of grace. The bride was in a sad condition in Song 5:2, asleep in complacency; but as soon as Christ speaks, she cries, “It is the voice of my beloved that knocketh!” She knew His voice, and was so familiar with fellowship with Him that she recognized Him at once. And so will you. If you train yourselves in acquaintance and fellowship with Him, you will easily tell the difference between His voice and the voice of a stranger. And take this κριτήριον, this test, with you: when He does speak, He speaks as no one ever spoke. He speaks with power, and one way or another He will make your hearts burn within you, as He did with the disciples (Luke 24). He does it by putting “in his hand by the hole of the door” (Song 5:4), His Spirit into your hearts to take hold of you.

Whoever has his senses trained to discern good and evil, having grown in judgment and experience by constantly observing the ways of Christ’s dealings, the manner of the Spirit’s workings and the effects He usually produces, is the best judge for himself in this case.

Secondly, if the word of the Lord does your soul good, He is speaking it: if it humbles, if it cleanses, and if it serves the purposes for which promises are given, namely to endear, to cleanse, to melt, and to bind to obedience and self-emptying. But this is not my business, and I shall not turn aside further in pursuing this direction. Without keeping it, sin will gain great advantages toward hardening the heart.

fields.title: Exercise Faith on Christ for the Killing of Your Sin
fields.body_html:
The general use of the directions above — The great direction for accomplishing the work aimed at: exercise faith on Christ — The several ways this may be done — Considering the fullness in Christ for relief — Great expectations from Christ — The grounds of these expectations: His mercy, His faithfulness — The outcome of such expectations, on Christ’s part and on the believer’s part — Faith to be exercised especially on the death of Christ, Rom. 6:3–6 — The work of the Spirit in this whole business.

Now, the considerations I have dwelt on so far are things preparatory to the work aimed at rather than things that will accomplish it. What I have aimed at so far is the heart’s proper preparation for the work itself, without which it will not be accomplished.

The directions for the work itself, I mean those that belong to it in particular, are very few. They are these:

1. Set faith to work on Christ for the killing of your sin. His blood is the great sovereign remedy for sin-sick souls. Live in this, and you will die a conqueror. Indeed, through the good providence of God, you will live to see your lust dead at your feet.

But you will say, “How is faith to work on Christ for this end and purpose?” I say, in several ways:

(1.) By faith, fill your soul with a proper consideration of the provision laid up in Jesus Christ for this very end and purpose: that all your lusts, including this very lust you are entangled with, may be put to death. By faith ponder this: though you are in no way able, in or by yourself, to gain the victory over your disorder, though you are even weary of fighting and quite ready to faint, there is still enough in Jesus Christ to give you relief (Phil. 4:13). What held up the prodigal, when he was ready to faint, was that there was still bread enough in his father’s house. Though he was far from it, it relieved and steadied him that it was there. In your greatest distress and anguish, consider that fullness of grace, those riches, those treasures of strength, might and help that are laid up in Him for our support (John 1:16; Col. 1:19). Let them come into your mind and stay there. Consider that God has exalted Him “to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel” (Acts 5:31); and if to give repentance, then to give mortification, without which repentance neither is nor can be. Christ tells us that we obtain cleansing grace by abiding in Him (John 15:3). To exercise faith on the fullness in Christ for our supply is an eminent way of abiding in Christ, for both our being grafted in and our abiding are by faith (Rom. 11:19–20). So let your soul be exercised by faith with thoughts and convictions like these: “I am a poor, weak creature; unstable as water, I cannot excel. This corruption is too strong for me, and is at the very point of ruining my soul, and I do not know what to do. My soul has become like parched ground and a home for jackals. I have made promises and broken them; vows and commitments have come to nothing. Many times I have been persuaded that I had won the victory and would be delivered, but I was deceived. So I see plainly that without some outstanding help and support I am lost, and will be overcome to the point of abandoning God altogether. But still, though this is my state and condition, let the hands that hang down be lifted up and the feeble knees be strengthened. See, the Lord Christ, who has all fullness of grace in His heart and all fullness of power in His hand, is able to slay all these enemies of His. There is enough provision in Him for my relief and help. He can take my drooping, dying soul and make me more than a conqueror. ‘Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the Lord, and my judgment is passed over from my God? Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding. He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: but they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint’ (Isa. 40:27–31). He can make the ‘parched ground’ of my soul ‘become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water.’ Indeed, He can make this ‘habitation of dragons,’ this heart so full of abominable lusts and fiery temptations, a place of ‘grass’ and of fruit for Himself” (Isa. 35:7). So God steadied Paul under his temptation by the thought of the sufficiency of His grace: “My grace is sufficient for thee” (2 Cor. 12:9). Though he was not immediately given so much of it as to be freed from his temptation, the sufficiency of it in God for that end and purpose was enough to steady his spirit. I say, then, by faith think much about the supply in Jesus Christ and its fullness, and how He can give you strength and deliverance at any time. Now, even if by this you do not find success amounting to victory, you will still be kept steady in the chariot, so that you do not flee from the field until the battle is over. You will be kept from utter despondency, from lying down under your unbelief, and from turning aside to false means and remedies that in the end will not relieve you. The power of this consideration will be found only in practice.

(2.) Lift up your heart by faith to an expectation of relief from Christ. Relief from Christ in this case is like the prophet’s vision: “For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry” (Hab. 2:3). Though it may seem rather long to you while you are under your trouble and distress, it will surely come at the time appointed by the Lord Jesus, which is the best time. If, then, you can lift your heart to a settled expectation of relief from Jesus Christ; if your eyes are toward Him “as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters,” when they expect to receive something from them; your soul will be satisfied. He will certainly deliver you. He will slay the lust, and your end will be peace. Only look for it from His hand, and wait for when and how He will do it. “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.”

But you will say, “What ground do I have to build such an expectation on, so that I may expect not to be deceived?”

As you have necessity driving you to this course, since you must be relieved and saved this way or not at all (for to whom will you go?), so there are countless things in the Lord Jesus to encourage you and draw you into this expectation.

As for its necessity, I have partly shown it already, when I made clear that this is the work of faith and of believers only. “Without me,” says Christ, “ye can do nothing” (John 15:5), speaking with particular reference to the cleansing of the heart from sin (verse 2). The putting to death of any sin must come by a supply of grace. We cannot do it by ourselves. Now, “it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell” (Col. 1:19), so that “of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace” (John 1:16). He is the head from whom the new man must receive influences of life and strength, or it will decline every day. If we are “strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man,” it is by Christ dwelling in our hearts by faith (Eph. 3:16–17). I have also shown before that this work cannot be done without the Spirit. Where, then, do we expect the Spirit from? From whom do we look for Him? Who has promised Him to us, having obtained Him for us? Ought not all our expectations in this matter to be fixed on Christ alone? So let this be fixed on your heart: if you do not have relief from Him, you will never have any. All ways, efforts and struggles that are not driven by this expectation of relief from Christ, and from Him alone, are to no purpose and will do you no good. Indeed, if they are anything other than supports for your heart in this expectation, or means He Himself has appointed for receiving help from Him, they are in vain.

Now, to draw you further into this expectation:

(1.) Consider His mercy, tenderness and kindness as our great High Priest at the right hand of God. He certainly pities you in your distress. He says, “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you” (Isa. 66:13). He has the tenderness of a mother toward a nursing child. “Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people. For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted” (Heb. 2:17–18). How is Christ’s ability, on account of His suffering, set before us? “In that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able.” Did Christ’s sufferings and temptations add to His ability and power? Certainly not, considered absolutely and in itself. But the ability mentioned here is one that comes with readiness, inclination and willingness to put itself out. It is an ability of will, against every argument to the contrary. Having suffered and been tempted, He is able to break through every argument to the contrary to relieve poor tempted souls. Δύναται βοηθῆσαι, “He is able to help.” It names the effect for the cause: now that He has been tempted like this, He can be moved to help. So too in 4:15–16: “For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” The exhortation of verse 16 is the same one I am pressing: that we should cherish expectations of relief from Christ, which the apostle there calls χάριν εἰς εὔκαιρον βοήθειαν, “grace for timely help.” “If ever help was timely,” says the soul, “it would be for me in my present condition. This is what I long for: grace for timely help. I am ready to die, to perish, to be lost for ever. Iniquity will prevail against me if help does not come.” The apostle says, “Expect this help, this relief, this grace from Christ.” Yes, but on what ground? On what he sets out in verse 15. And we may note that the word in verse 16 translated “obtain” is λάβωμεν. Ἵνα λάβωμεν ἔλεον, “that we may receive” mercy: fitting and timely help will come. I will say freely that this one thing, establishing the soul by faith in the expectation of relief from Jesus Christ because of His mercy as our High Priest, will do more to ruin your lust and disorder, and will have a better and quicker outcome, than all the most rigorous means of self-torment any of the children of men ever committed themselves to. Indeed, let me add that no soul ever did or ever will perish by the power of any lust, sin or corruption who could lift his soul by faith to an expectation of relief from Jesus Christ.

(2.) Consider the faithfulness of Him who has promised, which may lift you up and strengthen you in this waiting in expectation of relief. He has promised to relieve in cases like this, and He will keep His word to the uttermost. God tells us that His covenant with us is like the “ordinances” of heaven, the sun, moon and stars, which have their fixed courses (Jer. 31:36). That is why David said that he waited for relief from God “more than they that watch for the morning,” something that will certainly come in its appointed season. So will your relief from Christ. It will come in its season, like the dew and rain on parched ground, for He who has promised is faithful. There are countless particular promises to this purpose. Let the soul always be supplied with some of them that seem especially suited to its condition.

Now, two outstanding advantages always come with this expectation of help from Jesus Christ:

[1.] It draws Him into full and speedy help. Nothing draws a person’s heart more to be useful and helpful to another than that other’s expectation of help from him, if it has been rightly raised and encouraged by the one who is to give the relief. Our Lord Jesus has raised our hearts to this expectation by His kindness, care and promises. Surely our rising up to it must be a great inducement to Him to help us accordingly. The Psalmist gives us this as a tested maxim: “Thou, Lord, hast not forsaken them that seek thee.” Once the heart is won to rest in God and to lean on Him, He will certainly satisfy it. He will never be like water that fails, nor has He ever said to the seed of Jacob, “Seek ye me in vain.” If Christ is chosen as the foundation of our supply, He will not fail us.

[2.] It draws the heart to attend diligently to all the ways and means by which Christ usually communicates Himself to the soul, and so it brings in the real help of every grace and ordinance. Someone who expects anything from another applies himself to the ways and means by which it may be obtained. The beggar who expects alms lies at the door, or in the path, of the one he expects them from. The way and the means by which Christ communicates Himself are ordinarily His ordinances. Whoever expects anything from Him must wait on Him there. It is the expectation of faith that sets the heart to work. I am not speaking of an idle, groundless hope. Now, if there is any vigour, power and effectiveness in prayer or sacrament for this purpose of putting sin to death, a person will certainly have a share in all of it through this expectation of relief from Christ. For this reason I bring all particular exercises, by prayer, meditation and the like, under this heading, and so shall not dwell on them further. When they rest on this foundation and spring from this root, they are of unique use for this purpose, and not otherwise.

Now, for this direction on putting a prevailing disorder to death you may have a thousand “probatum est’s,” a thousand testimonies that it has been proved. Who has walked with God under this temptation and not found its use and success? I dare leave the soul with it without adding any more. Only some particulars connected with it may be mentioned:

First, exercise faith especially on the death, blood and cross of Christ, that is, on Christ as crucified and slain. The putting to death of sin comes especially from the death of Christ. It is one special, indeed one outstanding, purpose of the death of Christ, which will certainly be accomplished by it. He died to destroy the works of the devil. Whatever came on our nature through the devil’s first temptation, and whatever gains strength in our persons through his daily suggestions, Christ died to destroy it all. “Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works” (Titus 2:14). This was His aim and intention in giving Himself for us, and He will not fail in it. His design was that we might be freed from the power of our sins and purified from all our defiling lusts. “Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it... that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Eph. 5:25–27). And this will be accomplished, in various and different degrees, by the power of His death. That is why our washing, purging and cleansing are everywhere credited to His blood (1 John 1:7; Heb. 1:3; Rev. 1:5). When it is sprinkled on us, it purges our consciences “from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9:14). This is what we aim at and are pursuing: that our consciences may be purged from dead works, that they may be rooted out and destroyed and have no place in us any more. This will certainly be brought about by the death of Christ; power will go out from it for this purpose. Indeed, all supplies of the Spirit, all communications of grace and power, come from there, as I have shown elsewhere. So the apostle puts it. Rom. 6:2 states the very case we have in hand: “How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” “Dead to sin by profession; dead to sin by obligation to be so; dead to sin by sharing in the power and strength to kill it; dead to sin by union with and share in Christ, in whom and by whom it is killed: how shall we live in it?” He presses this in the following verses with several considerations, all drawn from the death of Christ. It must not be: “Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?” (verse 3). In baptism we have evidence of our being planted into Christ; we are baptized into Him. But what of His are we baptized into a share in? “His death,” he says. If we really are baptized into Christ, beyond outward profession, we are baptized into His death. The apostle explains what it is to be baptized into the death of Christ in verses 4 and 6: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life... Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.” “This,” he says, “is our being baptized into the death of Christ: our conformity to it; being dead to sin, having our corruptions put to death, as He was put to death for sin; so that as He was raised up to glory, we may be raised up to grace and newness of life.” In verse 6 he tells us where this baptism into the death of Christ comes from, and it is from the death of Christ itself: “our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed.” Συνεσταυρώθη, “is crucified with him,” not in respect of time but of cause. We are crucified with Him by merit, in that He obtained the Spirit for us to put sin to death; by power, in that power comes out from His death for our crucifying; and by way of representation and example, in that we shall certainly be crucified to sin, as He was for our sin. This is what the apostle means: Christ, by His death destroying the works of the devil and obtaining the Spirit for us, has so killed sin as to its reign in believers that it will not achieve its aim and dominion.

Secondly, then, exercise faith on the death of Christ in these two ways: first, in expectation of power; secondly, in efforts toward conformity. For the first, the general direction already given may be enough. For the second, the apostle’s words in Gal. 3:1 may give us some light for our direction. Let faith look on Christ in the gospel as He is set forth dying and crucified for us. Look on Him under the weight of our sins, praying, bleeding, dying. Bring Him into your heart by faith in that condition. Apply His blood, shed in this way, to your corruptions. Do this daily. I could draw this consideration out at great length in several particulars, but I must come to a close.

2. I have only to add, then, the main headings of the work of the Spirit in this business of mortification, which is credited to Him in such a special way.

In a word: this whole work, which I have described as our duty, is brought about, carried on and accomplished by the power of the Spirit, in all its parts and degrees. For example:

(1.) He alone clearly and fully convinces the heart of the evil, guilt and danger of the corruption, lust or sin that is to be put to death. Without this conviction, or while it is so faint that the heart can wrestle with it or digest it, no thorough work will be done. An unbelieving heart (and in part we all have one) will dodge any consideration until it is overpowered by clear and evident convictions. Now this is the proper work of the Spirit. “He will reprove the world of sin” (John 16:8); He alone can do it. If people’s reasoning, together with the preaching of the letter, could convince them of sin, we might perhaps see more convictions than we do. Through the preaching of the word an awareness comes on people’s understanding that they are sinners, that such and such things are sins, and that they themselves are guilty of them. But this light is not powerful. It does not take hold of the practical principles of the soul so as to conform the mind and will to them and produce effects that match such an awareness. That is why wise and knowledgeable people who lack the Spirit do not think of those things as sins at all in which the chief stirrings and workings of lust consist. It is the Spirit alone who can do this work effectively, and who does. And this is the first thing the Spirit does toward putting any lust whatever to death: He convinces the soul of all its evil, cuts off all its pleas, exposes all its deceptions, blocks all its evasions, answers its pretexts, makes the soul own its abomination and lie down under the sense of it. Unless this is done, everything that follows is in vain.

(2.) The Spirit alone reveals to us the fullness of Christ for our relief, and this is the consideration that keeps the heart from false ways and from despairing despondency (1 Cor. 2:8).

(3.) The Spirit alone establishes the heart in expectation of relief from Christ, which is the great sovereign means of mortification, as has been shown (2 Cor. 1:21).

(4.) The Spirit alone brings the cross of Christ into our hearts with its sin-killing power, for it is by the Spirit that we are baptized into the death of Christ.

(5.) The Spirit is the author and finisher of our sanctification. He gives new supplies and influences of grace for holiness and sanctification when the opposite principle is weakened and brought down (Eph. 3:16–18).

(6.) In all the soul’s approaches to God in this condition, it has support from the Spirit. Where does the power, life and vigour of prayer come from? Where does its power to prevail with God come from? Is it not from the Spirit? He is the “spirit of... supplications” promised to those who “look upon me whom they have pierced” (Zech. 12:10), enabling them to pray “with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Rom. 8:26). This is acknowledged to be the great means, or way, by which faith prevails with God. This is how Paul dealt with his temptation, whatever it was: “I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.” It is not my present purpose to show what the work of the Spirit in prayer is, from where and how He gives us His help and makes us prevail, and what we must do to enjoy His help for that purpose.
